item.title: Same-Sex Relations Decriminalized in Trinidad by a Court in Britain
item.description:
A ruling by a British-based court has invalidated laws criminalizing homosexuality in Trinidad and Tobago, setting a precedent for those challenging similar laws in other nations in the Caribbean and possibly beyond.

The ruling was handed down on Tuesday by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, which serves as the highest court of appeal for dozens of crown dependencies, overseas territories and former British colonies.

Five British judges unanimously upheld a 2018 decision by a lower court in Trinidad that had found two sections of the Caribbean country’s 1986 law targeting private, consensual same-sex relations to be unconstitutional. An appeals court in Trinidad had reversed the lower-court decision in 2025.

Trinidad’s attorney general had argued that the law preserved traditional family values in the country, and had leaned on a legal mechanism called “savings provisions,” which kept many laws from the British colonial era.

The decision delivered a hard-fought victory to advocates for L.G.B.T.Q. rights in Trinidad. Jason Jones, an L.G.B.T.Q. activist who had been a key plaintiff against the law since 2015, called the ruling a “vindication.” He said it would provide hope to young L.G.B.T.Q. people in his country who are living in fear of legal and societal discrimination.

Still, Mr. Jones noted ruefully, to challenge the colonial-era law, his lawyers had to seek intervention from a court based in Britain — decades after Trinidad gained independence, in 1962.

“We are a colonized people,” he said. “Why are we running to white people in London for our justice?”

Here’s what to know about the ruling.

During the colonial period, Britain imposed its system of laws across a global empire spanning nations in the Caribbean, Africa and Asia.

Many laws on the books in Trinidad and Tobago are left over from before the island nation of 1.5 million people left the British monarchy and became a republic in 1976. While laws criminalizing homosexuality in Trinidad stemmed from colonial-era legislation, they were amended to be even stricter in 1986.

Even as colonies became independent in the latter half of the 20th century, some retained deep economic, cultural and legal ties to Britain as part of an umbrella group of nations called the Commonwealth. It is made up of 56 members.

One of the vestiges of the British Empire is the Privy Council, which serves as the court of last resort for some of those nations. Caribbean countries have the power to leave the Privy Council system, said Téa Braun, chief executive of Human Dignity Trust, an international legal organization focused on eradicating anti-L.G.B.T.Q. laws. And many have done so, moving to regional bodies like the Caribbean Court of Justice.

Although the Caribbean court is headquartered in Trinidad’s capital, Port of Spain, the country has not made it the final court of appeal. And Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has said she has no imminent plans to do so.

Ria Mohammed, a Trinidadian lawyer and director of the Caribbean Center for Human Rights, said it was “deliciously ironic” that a British-based court had helped invalidate colonial-era laws. But she noted that Caribbean judges had also been major players in enacting similar changes across the region.

Mr. Jones, 62, who moved to Britain at the age of 21, said he had been frustrated by a legal apparatus that required change to come from outside Trinidad. But he said: “I will use any tool to fight. If systems exist, you have to work within those systems to dismantle them.”

The ruling was a source of deep personal pride for Mr. Jones, but it was also celebrated by rights groups in Trinidad and beyond that had supported his efforts.

“This victory is more than a legal milestone,” Pride TT, an L.G.B.T.Q. rights group in the country, said on social media on Tuesday. “It is a reminder that everyone deserves to live with dignity, privacy and freedom from discrimination.”

Alex Farrow, chief executive of Kaleidoscope Trust, a British-based charity for L.G.B.T.Q. causes, said in a statement: “Horrifyingly, the number of countries criminalizing homosexuality has been increasing over the past two years. To see that number fall yesterday is a huge achievement.”

The prime minister and attorney general did not respond to requests for comment on the decision. But homosexuality remains deeply stigmatized in the country, and some religious leaders in the country expressed disappointment in the ruling.

“I cannot tell anybody how to live their life,” Ellis Burris, president of the country’s Inter-Religious Organization, said in a phone interview. But he said he believed that homosexuality was “against the divine law.”

The ruling will not automatically cause anti-gay laws to be struck from the books in Trinidad, said Ms. Braun, the Human Dignity Trust executive. But she said they were now void and unenforceable.

And she said the ruling could be cited in challenges to similar laws in other countries that operate under the Commonwealth system, though its effect would be “persuasive, not binding.” Each nation has its own constitutional provisions.

Challenges to laws in, for example, Jamaica, Grenada, Guyana and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines could be bolstered by the Trinidad ruling, Ms. Braun said.

While Trinidadians were rarely charged under the laws, rights groups argue that striking them down helps insulate them from discrimination.

item.title: Indonesia’s Vice President Resigns as a Political Alliance Unravels
item.description:
The vice president of Indonesia submitted his resignation to Parliament on Thursday, succumbing to a scandal about his academic credentials and injecting new political uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka was elected as Indonesia’s youngest vice president in 2024, in a precipitous rise. He was a symbol of the partnership between his father, the outgoing president, Joko Widodo, and the incoming leader, Prabowo Subianto, that elevated Mr. Prabowo into office.

“The relationship has clearly fractured,” said Yoes C. Kenawas, a political analyst at the Indonesian Survey Institute. With Mr. Gibran’s departure, “Prabowo is attempting to demonstrate that he has stepped out from Jokowi’s shadow,” he added, referring to the former leader by his nickname.

Initially a political outsider, Mr. Joko came to be seen as a transformative leader of Indonesia. He helped rehabilitate the image of Mr. Prabowo, a former special forces commander who was discharged from the military for his involvement in the abduction and torture of pro-democracy activists under the dictator Suharto. To many, Mr. Prabowo was a reminder of the country’s authoritarian past. But Mr. Joko endorsed Mr. Prabowo as his successor, with Mr. Gibran running on the same ticket.

The alliance between Mr. Joko and Mr. Prabowo was cast as one of political continuity. Many voters had seen Mr. Gibran’s vice presidency as a way for Mr. Joko to continue his political influence.

“From the beginning, Gibran was brought on board solely to serve as a ‘vote-getter,’ rather than as an integral part of a unified leadership team intended to strengthen the performance of the Prabowo administration,” said Titi Anggraini, a lecturer of constitutional law at University of Indonesia.

Mr. Prabowo’s two years in office have been dominated by his authoritarian tilt and populist policies that have rattled the economy. In recent weeks his approval rating has plummeted, leaving the country in a combustible moment that evokes the ouster of Suharto three decades ago.

It was not immediately clear when Mr. Gibran’s resignation would be effective. He is stepping down after mounting calls for impeachment over allegations that he had failed to meet a requirement to run for office — holding the equivalent of a high-school diploma — even though he later earned a university degree.

Mr. Gibran has said that he finished grade 12 at a school in Australia. He has faced two cases, one that challenged his high school credentials and another that sought to remove him from office on the grounds that those credentials were illegitimate.

Last month, the Constitutional Court said that it had found no convincing evidence that Mr. Gibran possessed a foreign diploma equivalent to an Indonesian senior high school certificate. But it noted that it did not have the jurisdiction to unseat him directly.

Two weeks ago, the Supreme Court delivered another blow. It revoked a high school equivalency certificate that was issued to Mr. Gibran by the Education Ministry in 2019. But the justices did not establish that Mr. Gibran had forged a document, centering their ruling instead on administrative compliance.

Earlier this month, what appeared to be a seismic break in the Jokowi-Prabowo alliance emerged. Several officials, including Mr. Prabowo’s chief of staff, who were seen as close to Mr. Joko, were arrested on charges of wiretapping the president.

Mr. Joko appeared to cast a conciliatory note on Thursday.

“I have told Gibran that any position one holds is only temporary; positions are fleeting,” he told reporters. “We remain committed to supporting President Prabowo’s administration, especially regarding programs that benefit the broader public.”

The controversy that felled Mr. Gibran has an unusual family parallel.

Mr. Joko has faced claims that he doctored a university certificate to become eligible to run for office. Last week, Mr. Joko, appeared in a Jakarta courtroom to display his original diploma from Gadjah Mada University, seeking to rebut long-running allegations regarding its authenticity.

The Constitutional Court played a crucial role in Mr. Gibran’s ascendance to the vice presidency. In a 5-4 decision in 2023, it carved out an exception to the minimum age requirement of 40 for presidential and vice-presidential candidates, allowing younger candidates who had held elected regional office to run. Mr. Gibran, now 39, had been the mayor of the city of Surakarta.

The deciding vote was cast by Chief Justice Anwar Usman, who had been appointed by Mr. Joko and later married the president’s sister. Soon after, an ethics panel removed Mr. Anwar from his post, citing a conflict of interest, but it could not overturn the court’s decision.

item.title: In China’s Spy Operations, Romance Can Be a Long Game
item.description:
At the height of the Cold War, a top official in China’s intelligence agency said that his country would never use seduction to entrap a person.

Such tactics might be for the C.I.A. or the K.G.B., the official named Kong Yuan, of the Central Investigation Department, told a group of agents in training in April 1960, but China was guided by principles. He looked at the few female comrades in the audience. “Rest assured, we will not be asking you to go run beauty traps.”

Despite that pledge, captured in a 2010 memoir by a former Chinese diplomat, China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people.

American officials say that China’s Ministry of State Security, which runs intelligence operations today, recruited a Chinese businesswoman to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and one of the most powerful figures in the artificial intelligence boom.

It was not clear what role the woman, Alice Huang, or Huang Le, might have had with the Chinese spy agency. Ms. Huang was a top executive of a Singapore company that operates data centers in Southeast Asia using Nvidia chips and that rents their computing power to Chinese firms.

Mr. Huang has acknowledged that he had an affair with Ms. Huang. President Trump has said that Mr. Huang told him that he was not aware that the woman was a spy. China has rejected the espionage allegations against Ms. Huang, calling them smears against the country. U.S. officials have not provided evidence for their claims. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

The use of relationships or seduction in the world of espionage is not new or unique to China. The tactic was made infamous by East Germany’s “Romeos,” male Stasi agents tasked with seducing the clerks of Western officials, and by the Soviet Union’s longtime use of sexual blackmail, among other examples.

What is unique about China’s use of the tactic is the amount of time invested, according to Nicholas Eftimiades, a retired senior American intelligence officer who writes about China’s espionage operations.

“They play this long term,” he said. “These are long-term relationships, sometimes marriages.”

Perhaps the most famous example involves Shi Peipu, a Peking Opera singer whose two-decade relationship with Bernard Boursicot, who worked on French diplomatic missions in Beijing and Ulan Bator in Mongolia, drew Mr. Boursicot into spying for China. Both were arrested in France, at which point Mr. Boursicot learned that his lover was a man. In 1986, they were convicted of espionage. Their story inspired the play “M. Butterfly” by David Henry Hwang.

More recent cases include Christine Fang, or Fang Fang, who was believed by counterintelligence officials to be a Chinese spy and who was in a physical relationship with former U.S. Representative Eric Swalwell between 2012 and 2015.

Separately, a retired U.S. Army officer who was working as a contractor for the U.S. Pacific Command in Hawaii was sentenced to prison in 2014 for emailing defense secrets, including details about joint training exercises between the United States and South Korea, to a 27-year-old Chinese woman with whom he had been involved romantically for almost two years.

In 2003, an F.B.I. agent, James J. Smith, who worked in Chinese counterintelligence, admitted that he had an affair for nearly 20 years with a Chinese American businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese double agent. The woman, whom he had recruited as an asset, was found to have given classified U.S. government information to Beijing.

Both the United States and China appear to be concerned about the possibility of emotional or other manipulation by the other side. Last year, the U.S. government prohibited American personnel in China from having romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens, according to The Associated Press.

China’s intelligence agency itself frequently warns its citizens to look out for foreign operatives attempting to trap them. In May, China’s Ministry of State Security published an article on WeChat that called on residents to “be wary of sudden advances and overt displays of affection from seemingly perfect individuals of the opposite sex.”

“Avoid falling into the ‘gentle trap,’” it said.

Alex Joske, managing director at Garnaut Global, an advisory firm, said the Chinese ministry’s warnings about espionage “are usually based on the kinds of things that they do rather than what other countries actually do.”

Compared with Western intelligence agencies, the Chinese government is more willing to use blackmail and coercion in its operations, including romance and sexual activities, he argued. Western governments see blackmail as a less reliable way of motivating a source or asset, he said.

China’s Ministry of State Security, which oversees operations abroad as well as security within the country, is known for its highly coercive methods that include threats of arrest and detention.

The agency also exploits other forms of relationships, like family ties. A former F.B.I. agent in New York was recruited, with the help of his mother in China, to pass information about the agency to Beijing. He pleaded guilty to the charges in 2016.

China does engage in the kind of sexually baited entrapment one might see in a spy drama, according to former American intelligence officers. “A diplomat walks into his hotel room, and there’s a girl in his bed. I mean, that stuff happens. It’s just kind of ridiculous,” Mr. Eftimiades said.

Dennis Wilder, who was senior China director at the National Security Council during the George W. Bush administration and a former senior intelligence officer, describes how when he traveled to Beijing, a woman would often be waiting in the elevator for him when he returned to his hotel.

“She’d say, ‘You know, I can come to your room.’ And I’d say, ‘Well why do you want to come to my room?’ And they did this over and over again to see if they could get me,” he said, noting that if he was ever to publicly accuse the Chinese of trying to entrap him, they could say the women were prostitutes working on their own volition.

“That’s the beauty of this kind of thing. It’s totally deniable,” Mr. Wilder said.

But more often than not, Mr. Eftimiades said, Beijing is not sending operatives to stage romantic encounters for blackmail. Instead, it looks for people whose personal or professional lives give them access to potential targets, he said.

Many details of the relationship between Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang, including when they met and under what circumstances Ms. Huang may have begun gathering information for Beijing, remain unclear.

China’s large diaspora includes executives, students and others who can be recruited in what Mr. Eftimiades calls the country’s “whole of society” approach to espionage.

Of the many cases of Chinese spying that have come to light over the past few years, only a handful involve romantic relationships. In most cases, the best motivation is money, Mr. Joske says. But when it comes to targeting wealthy elites, money is not always as powerful a recruitment tool.

“So instead, you try to co-opt someone in their circle,” he said. That includes someone with whom that person has a close relationship.

A close relationship is also conducive to another major goal of China’s intelligence operations, which is to exert influence on key decision makers or gather information to sway other prominent figures to support policies favorable to Beijing.

“Once you become emotionally involved with somebody, your base line judgment changes,” said Matthew Brazil, a senior fellow at The Jamestown Foundation focusing on Chinese intelligence operations. “People want to please their lovers.”

David Pierson in Hong Kong and Pei-Lin Wu in Taipei contributed reporting.

item.title: The End of Russia’s Bravest Newspaper
item.description:
Novaya Gazeta was a newspaper of near-legendary status in Russia. It was the home of the investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, whose books in the early 2000s offered a searing account of human rights abuses, wartime propaganda and corruption in Vladimir Putin’s Russia. In 2006, on Putin’s birthday, Politkovskaya was shot and killed in the elevator of her apartment building. Twenty years later, Russia is back at war and Novaya Gazeta has shut down.

On Monday, the paper held its last editorial meeting. One final issue will come out in the next few weeks. I spoke to my colleague Valerie Hopkins, who was there to witness the journalists packing up their offices.

But first, the latest twist in the Nvidia scandal: Jensen Huang has resigned.

Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia, resigned on Thursday, capping the swift, stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. He had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was spying for China, and with an executive who reported to him.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive while the search for a permanent chief executive is carried out. Nvidia shares dropped as much as 14 percent, extending a decline that has wiped out more than $1 trillion from its market capitalization in the last month. Follow our live coverage here.

Here’s a visual guide to understanding the scandal:

Valerie, Novaya Gazeta, the last big independent Russian media organization, closed its newsroom this week. The paper and its journalists have been under intense pressure from President Vladimir Putin for decades. Why now?

The real miracle is that they lasted this long. We’ve watched the Russian government systematically dismantle any media organization that is critical of the Kremlin and critical of the war in Ukraine. This didn’t happen overnight.

First their website was blocked, so you needed a VPN to read them. Then they lost their media license. Then Putin signed a decree nationalizing their printing presses. Then this spring, authorities raided the newsroom and one of their journalists was detained and put on trial. The paper was added to the list of so-called foreign agents — this kind of Stalin-era term that comes with many limitations on what you’re allowed to do.

There was this idea that eventually they would give up, but they didn’t. What ultimately forced them to close was when their landlord refused to renew their lease after 20 years and their bank stopped processing the reader donations that were their only remaining source of revenue. They went to other banks saying, Will you help us? But everyone said no. And that’s a function of either direct pressure from the authorities, or the understanding that you’re going to have a problem if you keep working with the paper.

And so they made the decision that they couldn’t go on any longer.

Explain why this paper was so important in Russia.

It was known, above all, for the bravery of its journalists. They were never silenced, despite years of intimidation, attacks, pressure, assassinations.

Six of its journalists have been killed. Shortly after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the paper’s editor, Dmitri Muratov, was attacked on a train. The attack was so bad that he needed four operations to use his eyes again.

The other reason Novaya Gazeta was so important was that at a time when many antiwar Russians and antiwar journalists left Russia, they stayed. They remained on the ground, living in their readers’ reality. That meant a great deal.

You were in that newsroom during its last day on Monday. What was it like?

It certainly felt like the end of an era. You know, these are people who are full of tremendous love and respect for the craft of journalism. But during that final editorial meeting on Monday, there was also this discussion about the fact that despondency is a sin, as one of the paper’s columnists wrote. He’s an Orthodox priest who was stripped of his congregation for his antiwar stance. So the sadness of the moment was mixed with defiance and pride in having lasted this long.

One of the things I found very moving was the description in your article of Anna Politkovskaya’s office, which had become a kind of museum and is now gone.

Yes, it’s heartbreaking. They saved her office almost as it was when she was killed. They kept her tape recorder, some of her letters, her really old-school computer. Her reading glasses were still on her desk. And then on the wall they had some of her best stories and also an investigation that her colleagues did into her assassination. It was a place where young journalists would come to be inspired. But all of that is going in storage.

I want to come back to the fact that they lasted this long. How did they manage to do it?

They were strategic. They decided, OK, we’re here, we need to follow Russian law. That meant they didn’t write about anything happening on the front line in Ukraine because there are laws in place that make it illegal to cite any sources besides the Ministry of Defense. But they also made it very clear that they weren’t writing about the front lines because of censorship. For instance, they would use the word “war” on their front pages, instead of the state-approved “special military operation,” but deliberately blur it out.

Another thing that might have helped protect them somewhat was the moral weight of their co-founder sharing the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. And the moral authority of their history: The paper was founded with money from the Nobel Peace Prize Mikhail Gorbachev won. Muratov was close to Gorbachev, and he also knows a lot of prominent decision makers, including in Putin’s government. But as this war goes on, as the screws are being tightened, that will only get you so far.

Is there any other independent news outlet left in Russia now?

There are some, mostly on Telegram, but none of them with this kind of authority and weight. You know, as recently as a few months ago, Novaya Gazeta’s journalists were going to occupied territory in Ukraine. They went to Oleshky, the Russian-controlled city where people were starving, and wrote about it. The type of stuff that Novaya Gazeta was doing, nobody else is doing.

And what will their journalists do now?

I don’t think they plan to emigrate. Maybe they will eventually try to start something new. I think they’re all still trying to figure it out.

Read Valerie’s story in full.

The Israeli military struck a hospital in southern Gaza, killing at least six people and injuring 28 more, according to local health officials. Israel said it was targeting a Hamas commander.

President Trump said that he had pulled Vice President JD Vance back from peace talks with Iran, saying, “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”

Iran is seizing assets from some citizens because they have family members living abroad who have criticized the government.

Trump’s envoys went to Moscow to seek agreement from Putin to bring Europe into talks on the war in Ukraine.

A court in the U.K. decriminalized homosexuality in Trinidad and Tobago, where the legal system is intertwined with the former colonial power.

In Peru, where Pope Leo lived for two decades, he’s meeting ghosts from his past.

In Malawi, El Niño is expected to bring extreme weather and a possible famine. Our global climate correspondent Chico Harlan visited a remote village to see how farmers are preparing for an imminent drought.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about the death of Russia’s ambassador to the U.S.

The world is full of wild creatures doing secret things. For nearly all of history, those lives stayed hidden. Now, hundreds of thousands of viewers can watch two bald eagles fight to raise a family. Climb inside their nest.

Ukrainians have learned to distrust their GPS: It keeps telling them they’re in Peru.

The cause is a Ukrainian system that blasts out electromagnetic interference meant to confuse Russian missiles and drones, making them think they are somewhere else. Sometimes, the weapons are so confused that they make severe turns and break apart midair.

But the system is also disrupting civilians’ everyday lives. One person using a ride-hailing app was told that she’d be home in 12,276 minutes. Read more.

Advent mania: The holiday calendars are now a billion-dollar industry, hiding everything from pickles to protein powder behind their doors.

Lost invention: Greek fire was an incendiary weapon developed in the seventh century and used for more than 500 years before the recipe was lost.

Accidentally viral: The song “Talafreako,” by a little-known Texas rapper, became an unlikely anthem for Senator-elect James Talarico.

This fluffy, custardy banana pudding scented with cardamom is light enough to linger over after a big feast. Be sure to make it the day before serving so that the vanilla wafers can fully hydrate.

Where is this mountain village?

Azerbaijan

Nepal

Lesotho

Taiwan

This week I went to the opening night of “Owain & Henry,” an epic historical drama about a medieval Welsh prince leading a rebellion against English rule in the 15th century. Stay with me.

The production was unlike any other celebration of a national story I’ve seen before.

It wasn’t “Braveheart,” where the 14th-century Scottish war hero William Wallace famously cried “Freedom!” just before being executed — but ultimately inspired his countrymen to win their independence from England.

And it wasn’t “Hamilton,” where America’s founding fathers won their independence from England and wrote the most ambitious constitution in history (while rapping about it).

The Welsh never did regain their independence from England. But any nation-building exercise worth its salt needs to land on a note of triumph somehow. And so “Owain & Henry” instead chose to celebrate values like roots, community, mercy — and holding on to a strong national identity. As Prince Owain Glyndwr, played by the great Michael Sheen, puts it: “We are still here.” It was a reminder that nation-building, and the human instinct to find meaning and comfort in our national identities, can take many forms.

(I will say it was long. Over three hours. It could have done with a trim. The journalist in me was thinking: Get an editor.)

Speaking of “We are still here” (or “Yma o hyd” in Welsh) — I’ve always loved “O Hyd” by the Welsh rapper Sage Todz. I’ve recommended it before, and I’m recommending it again.

Have a great weekend! — Katrin

item.title: Army Officer Accused of Trying to Spy for Russia Is Afghan War Veteran
item.description:
A U.S. Army officer arrested in Britain on suspicion of trying to spy for Russia is a decorated veteran of the Afghanistan war who was caught in a sting operation, according to two American officials familiar with the case.

The suspect, Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested this week. British officials are expected to charge him on Sunday or Monday, and after that, the U.S. Army will seek to charge him under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and transfer him to the United States, the two officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing inquiry.

Beyond the sting, it was not clear what actions prompted Colonel Tyner’s arrest. He was based at the headquarters of NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, about 100 miles west of London. The base is NATO’s largest in Britain and hosts troops from 20 allied nations responsible for rapid response to crises.

In a statement announcing the arrest, the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel, said the case involved “allegations of espionage.” Though officials said in a statement that “the country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” it is unclear whether Colonel Tyner actually handed over sensitive information to Moscow.

Cellphone numbers for Colonel Tyner and his wife were disconnected. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that he had been caught in a sting.

The Kremlin has denied any involvement. “This arrest has nothing to do with us and we don’t know what it is connected to,” the Kremlin’s spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said at a news conference on Wednesday.

Colonel Tyner has been enlisted as a senior human resources officer in the Army since January 2008 and was deployed to Afghanistan for a year starting in December 2013. He also served in Iraq in 2019 and 2020 and Qatar before that. He is the recipient of a Bronze Star Medal and the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, among other awards.

His LinkedIn page indicates that he received a bachelor’s degree in criminology from the University of North Carolina at Pembroke.

In Britain, counterterrorism police have investigated several high-profile terrorism cases related to the United States in the past months, including two cases of arrests near air bases in England where the American military operates.

On Tuesday, federal prosecutors in the United States said that the commander of a powerful Iranian-backed militia helped direct a plot while sitting in a Brooklyn prison against R.A.F. Fairford, a military airfield used by American bombers in the war against Iran. In September, five men were arrested and then later released on bail near the base in connection with the plot.

Separately, two Latvian men were arrested in October on suspicion of a national security offense after breaching the perimeter of R.A.F. Molesworth, about 70 miles north of London, in Cambridgeshire, England.

British police said the arrest of Colonel Tyner was not related to those cases.

item.title: Mexican Prosecutor Who Helped C.I.A. Secretly Operate in His State Flees to the U.S.
item.description:
A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.

The former prosecutor, Guillermo Zuany Portillo, shepherded C.I.A. officers for more than six months beginning last year as they trained forces in his state, Chihuahua, joined those forces on counter-cartel missions and provided expertise during ground operations, a New York Times investigation revealed this week.

Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, had repeatedly said she did not want U.S. forces taking part in operations on the ground in Mexico, calling it a breach of sovereignty. Under the Trump administration, meanwhile, the C.I.A. sought to expand its activity in the country, and saw Mr. Zuany as a partner to help it do so quietly.

The C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua was blown when a car crash in April resulted in the deaths of two C.I.A. officers, leading to a national scandal and Mr. Zuany’s resignation. While an investigation determined the crash an accident, the Mexican authorities recently issued a warrant for Mr. Zuany’s arrest on charges related to his involvement with the agency.

Ms. Sheinbaum expressed fury at the C.I.A.’s presence during raids in Chihuahua and denied knowledge of the agency’s activities. On Wednesday, she said in a regular morning news conference that investigations into matter must continue.

“It’s worth finding out who this person is and how he worked with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said of Mr. Zuany.

The Mexican authorities also recently arrested Mr. Zuany’s former boss, Chihuahua’s former attorney general, César Jáuregui, on charges of treason, accusing him of welcoming the American intelligence agency into the state.

The U.S. government canceled Mr. Zuany’s U.S. visa late last year, accusing him of ties to Mexican cartels in Chihuahua, according to a letter the Mexican government sent to the F.B.I. and people familiar with Mr. Zuany’s visa status.

They and the officials spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment on Mr. Zuany’s case.

Mr. Zuany did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

After he facilitated the C.I.A.’s partnership with Mexican forces in Chihuahua, Mr. Zuany’s visa was reinstated late last year, Mexican and American officials said.

The F.B.I. had been investigating Mr. Zuany, who is accused of having ties to organized crime, according to the letter from the Mexican government. But the status of the case is unclear. The F.B.I. did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

Mr. Zuany recently fled to the United States to avoid capture, Mexican and American officials said, after Chihuahua state police officers arrested Mr. Jáuregui, who is now in a Mexican maximum-security prison.

As of Thursday, Mr. Zuany’s whereabouts in the United States were unclear.

The Mexican federal government also issued an order for Mr. Zuany’s arrest, according to the security minister, Omar García Harfuch, who revealed the information at a daily news conference, in response to The Times’s investigation.

In a statement, the office of Maru Campos, the governor of Chihuahua, said that the accusations against Mr. Zuany and Mr. Jáuregui represent “a serious failure” and that “she has taken responsibility for correcting the controls that made it possible.”

For months, a C.I.A. officer observed Chihuahua state agents practice tactical drills, analyzed their equipment and joined workouts, Mexican officials said. C.I.A. officers also joined Mr. Zuany and police units on operations against drug trafficking targets in the state.

In some cases, the C.I.A. officers were armed while on missions in Mexico, according to Mexican officials who were present.

On the way to one mission in March, Mr. Zuany and an American believed to be a C.I.A. officer discussed how to position state agents, a Chihuahua official told state prosecutors, according to an arrest-warrant request for Mr. Zuany. On another occasion, a C.I.A. officer carried a rifle and provided security as state police entered safe houses in search of drug traffickers, according to Mexican officials who were present.

The Americans generally wore tactical gear and were sometimes armed during the operations. In several cases, they wore jackets with Chihuahua state insignia, according to the warrant request and officials who had witnessed them. They also frequently carried computers or tablets during operations for what appeared to be real-time information, according to the warrant request and the officials.

The C.I.A. officers did not engage in combat, but instead mostly appeared to provide intelligence and direction, often via Mr. Zuany, the warrant request and officials said.

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

item.title: Nvidia C.E.O. Scandal Sets Off a Blitz of A.I. Memes
item.description:
Jensen Huang and his leather-clad likeness had become synonymous with the technological giant he co-founded, Nvidia. They were so entwined that, this year, the company sold $178 sweaters with a pixel-art version of Mr. Huang on the front.

Now, in the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday after back-to-back cheating scandals, including an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy, the internet has taken ahold of his image to unleash a flood of memes.

In many cases, they are being made by A.I. enthusiasts who revered Mr. Huang.

Images of Mr. Huang have appeared in online parodies of music videos, Bollywood movies, American sitcoms and kiss-cams at Coldplay concerts — many generated using artificial intelligence, the technology that became widely available through the chips Nvidia produces.

The revelations about Mr. Huang, 63, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom, are part of a long list of infidelity scandals that became memes.

Last year, the married chief executive of a tech start-up was caught on a kiss-cam at a Coldplay concert embracing the married but separated head of his company’s human resources department.

Mr. Huang’s image was superimposed on that viral moment by Peter Dedene, a Belgian software engineer. He said in a phone interview on Thursday that he was up late this week on his phone, scrolling the headlines about Nvidia.

Without leaving his bed, Mr. Dedene, 43, used an open-source generative A.I. tool to substitute the couple from the Coldplay concert with images of Mr. Huang and Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Mr. Huang has admitted having an affair.

“I didn’t think a lot of it,” Mr. Dedene said of his meme.

When he woke up on Sunday morning, he said, the post had over a million impressions. As of Thursday afternoon, it had nearly seven million.

“I really looked up to this guy,” Mr. Dedene said of Mr. Huang, adding, “It’s sort of hilarious that, in the end, the technology he cocreated is now enabling these kinds of jokes.”

Social media users have used A.I. to place Mr. Huang in iconic music videos about cheating.

In one post, Mr. Huang, donning his signature black leather jacket, takes Usher’s place in his music video for “Confessions, Pt. II.” (The lip-syncing is better in the original version.)

Thomas Unise, an A.I. consultant in Minneapolis who made the video, said it took him five minutes to find four images of Mr. Huang on Google and feed them into an A.I. tool to substitute Mr. Huang’s image for Usher’s in the video.

Mr. Unise, 40, said the proliferation of memes using Mr. Huang’s image illustrated how rapidly the technology had advanced.

“A year and a half ago, Will Smith eating spaghetti looked like a bunch of smears all over the screen,” he said of the actor and musician. “You can watch a video now and be like, ‘Wow, this actually looks pretty dang real.’”

In another video, Mr. Huang plays the character Neo in a scene from the movie “The Matrix.” President Trump, as the character Morpheus, lectures him on the importance of maintaining strategic competition with China and not falling for the woman in the red dress.

Mr. Huang’s avatar turns around to realize that the woman, replaced with an image of Ms. Huang, has become Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, brandishing a gun.

Elon Musk also makes a cameo in the meme, which as of Thursday had more than six million views on X.

On the theme of high-stakes deceit in Silicon Valley, some users placed Mr. Huang into “You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder who went to prison for defrauding investors.

With the help of generative A.I., users recast a montage from the documentary’s trailer in which Ms. Huang — as Ms. Holmes — unblinkingly insists, “Of course I’m not deceiving you.”

Many of the videos have labels identifying them as artificially generated.

But it’s “still surprising,” Mr. Dedene said of his video, how many people asked: “‘Is this real?’”

Ephrat Livni contributed reporting.

item.title: Paul Barril, French ‘Supergendarme’ Turned Mercenary, Has Died
item.description:
Paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”

Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).

Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.

His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.

By the time he founded his mercenary-security company, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.

In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a new military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.

In 1982, he became part of President François Mitterrand’s special antiterrorism police unit. That year, Mr. Barril was implicated in a murky affair in which he was alleged to have having planted weapons and explosives in the apartment of Irish nationalists in Vincennes, near Paris. French judicial authorities dropped the court case in 2002 on legal technicalities.

“We did the operation. We prevented bloodshed. I don’t acknowledge anything, ever,” Mr. Barril said on the French television program “Tout Le Monde En Parle” in 2000. “I would do the same thing all over again.”

It was in Africa that Mr. Barril gained the reputation that was to keep him at the center of French newspaper investigations, judicial probes and human-rights group complaints for decades.

With another former colleague from the gendarmerie, Mr. Barril was “at the service of the principal despotic governments of Africa and the Middle East, under the forgiving eye of the French security services,” according to the 2021 book “The Empire That Won’t Die: A History of Françafrique,” written by a collective of historians, journalists and human rights activists.

The book called Mr. Barril and his former colleague “emblematic figures” of “Françafrique,” a term employed in France and Africa to designate the murky official and unofficial networks — military, financial and political — entangling France with its former colonies. In 1990, Mr. Barril, for instance, recruited 15 mercenaries to teach the police in Gabon how to use tear gas against demonstrators, according to the book.

His connections with the Hutu government of Rwanda, responsible for the 1994 genocide in which close to one million Tutsis were murdered, earned him his greatest scrutiny.

In 2013, the Human Rights League of France, Survie, a human rights organization, and the International Federation for Human Rights accused him of “complicity in genocide” for supplying weapons and training to the Hutus. French magistrates investigated Mr. Barril’s role in Rwanda for years but never charged him.

Mr. Barril didn’t deny being in Rwanda at the time of the genocide. During a search of the Paris offices of his company, the French authorities found a May 1994 contract signed by Mr. Barril and the Rwandan prime minister in which Mr. Barril committed to supplying the Hutu government with “20 men for training purposes,” “two million cartridges” of varying calibers, “shells and mortars” and “grenades.”

The contract, which noted a fee of $3.13 million, was a violation of the United Nations arms embargo on Rwanda, and it was evidence that his men were helping the killers.

In June 1994, the Rwandan government paid him $1.2 million of the sum, according to Human Rights Watch; but before the contract could be fully carried out, Paul Kagame, who led a Tutsi-dominated rebel group and later became president, entered Kigali, the capital, on July 4, 1994, and halted the killing by the Hutus.

“There were three million dead” during the Rwandan civil war, Mr. Barril said on a television program six years later. “It’s the greatest historical lie ever. They’ve put it over that one ethnic group massacred another, when really, it was the opposite.”

Mr. Barril always hinted to investigators that he had been acting under the indirect direction of President Mitterrand’s administration, which had been allied with Rwanda’s Hutu government.

But his former boss in the GIGN, Christian Prouteau, said in an interview that Mr. Barril’s claims were nonsense.

“He had no mission, despite what he pretended subsequently,” Mr. Prouteau said. “As soon as he left the gendarmerie, at no moment whatsoever did he have a mandate from France.”

“He passed from the light to the darkness,” Mr. Prouteau added.

Paul Barril, the son and grandson of gendarmes, was born on April 13, 1946, in Vinay, in the Vercors region in southeastern France. He spent his childhood in the high Alps, the area where his father was posted.

At 18, Mr. Barril joined the army, was assigned to a tank unit in West Berlin, then returned to France for training at the gendarme sub-officers’ school, emerging top of his class. He went back to West Berlin, where one of his missions was to guard Rudolf Hess, the last remaining Nazi war criminal at Spandau Prison.

Mr. Barril took pity on the old man and, in the first of his memoirs, “Missions Très Spéciales” (1984), fantasized about liberating him. In 1975, he graduated from the gendarmes officer-training school in Melun, France, again at the top of his class.

Not long after Mr. Prouteau helped organize the GIGN in the 1970s, Mr. Barril presented himself in his office, and he became the older officer’s second in command. “He was a flamboyant young officer, brilliant and courageous,” Mr. Prouteau recalled. “He made some dangerous arrests, without arms.”

Things turned sour with the scandal over the arrest of the Irish militants. Twenty years later, Mr. Barril was caught up in another state scandal dating from those years: He received a six-month suspended sentence in 2005 and a fine for having been part of an illegal wiretapping ring in which dozens of politicians, actors, journalists, union leaders and others were bugged during the Mitterrand years.

“You’re not necessarily bugging people to hurt them,” Mr. Barril said on the 2000 television program.

In the meantime, according to Mr. Prouteau, Mr. Barril had gained a considerable fortune working for the emir of Qatar, among others, until illness overtook him at the beginning of the 2010s.

Mr. Barril is survived by his wife, Angélique, and his son, Patrick.

“He always had a nasty relationship with money,” Mr. Prouteau recalled. “And he was fascinated by mercenaries.”

After Mr. Prouteau was shot during a 1980 GIGN operation, he added: “Paul was in the hospital every day. Then, he became the other Barril. I can’t accept that.”

Daphné Anglès contributed research.

]]>

item.title: Lutnick Took a Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew
item.description:
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.

Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.

The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.

The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.

The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.

Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

Mr. Lutnick frequently calls and messages with Mr. Huang, and the department prepares carefully for their private meetings together in Mr. Lutnick’s fifth floor office. All Nvidia matters are routed through Jeff Kessler, a top deputy to Mr. Lutnick, who is said to rarely take any significant action without the commerce secretary’s approval.

Nvidia’s general counsel has also been given direct access to shape new rules, including leaving comments in draft regulations affecting the company.

Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, is known within the Commerce Department for his aggressive outreach. An inquiry inside the agency into whether Megaspeed was smuggling Nvidia chips into China was shut down late last year and transferred to the Justice Department after Mr. Teter reached out directly to Commerce Department investigators, invoking Mr. Kessler’s name in doing so.

Mr. Trump’s close relationship with Mr. Huang has also made department officials wary of taking aggressive steps to rein in sales of Nvidia chips, out of concern about angering Mr. Lutnick or the White House, according to interviews with current and former officials and others familiar with the policies, who discussed internal deliberations on the condition of anonymity.

In the wake of the revelations about Mr. Huang, the frictions within the administration about how to deal with Nvidia’s interests erupted last week. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Mr. Lutnick during a White House meeting over his handling of Megaspeed, demanding to know why the United States had not already banned chip sales to the company.

Mr. Lutnick responded that new measures could be put in place soon.

A spokeswoman for the Commerce Department denied that the interaction happened and said that the department had worked in concert with other agencies to issue export controls. She also denied that Mr. Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang had put a chill on the department’s actions, calling the idea “false and reckless.”

The spokeswoman, who declined to be named, said the department had charged defendants in multiple major criminal investigations targeting billions of dollars of chip smuggling, and imposed a license requirement on Nvidia’s H20 chip, unlike the Biden administration.

Nvidia declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

The Commerce Department has not always been so cautious on export controls. In Mr. Lutnick’s confirmation hearing in January last year, he promised to take a tough stance on oversight of technology sales to China.

“We need to stop helping them,” he said, referring to China’s progress in A.I. “I’m going to be very strong on that.”

But his critics say he has since been described as one of the biggest impediments to tighter rules.

Mr. Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have all had concerns about the sale of Nvidia’s advanced chips to China and have pushed for tighter restrictions.

But Mr. Lutnick has repeatedly delayed or deferred technology controls, slowing down efforts throughout the year, according to people who described the discussions.

In October, a few weeks before the midterm elections, some top officials in the Trump administration hoped to move forward with sweeping rules that would restrict Chinese companies from access to A.I. computing power in Southeast Asia, what some view as a major loophole in U.S. technology restrictions.

While the United States still bars the most advanced chips from being exported directly to China, Chinese companies have been able to gain access to them freely by remotely logging on to data centers in Southeast Asia. This is the business that Megaspeed, the Singaporean firm that was led by Ms. Huang, is engaged in.

The Biden administration issued regulations in January 2025 to clamp down on this issue, known as remote access, but the Trump administration rolled them back shortly after coming into office. Since then, officials have sparred over what to replace them with.

Both the State and Treasury Departments were in favor of moving forward with restrictions. The president had also signed off on the proposal.

Trump officials had just approached Oracle, which operates data centers in Southeast Asia, to try to dissuade it from pursuing a $7 billion deal to lease advanced chips to the Chinese company Tencent. Oracle agreed to cancel the deal, but told officials that its competitors were continuing to provide America’s most advanced computing power to Chinese companies.

Mr. Trump knew the step would affect Nvidia and Mr. Huang, but he had the support of most of his government advisers, as well as Elon Musk of Tesla and Mark Zuckerberg of Meta.

Then Mr. Kessler weighed in, saying that Mr. Lutnick had substantial policy issues with the idea. And Mr. Lutnick told his colleagues that he didn’t understand the rush.

The regulation was a serious issue that would affect other countries, as well as Nvidia, Mr. Lutnick said. He stressed to the team of Susie Wiles, then the White House chief of staff, that he believed any new action would instigate a further trade war with China and that he needed to have additional discussions with the president.

The Commerce Department spokeswoman said that the department was actively considering new rules to address remote access, along with other agencies.

The frustrations about Mr. Lutnick’s position on export controls are part of a larger battle between the commerce secretary and many others in the Trump White House and cabinet that dates to the presidential transition in late 2024. Mr. Lutnick led the effort, and his approach — seen by his internal critics as heavy-handed — earned him few fans.

Mr. Lutnick pushed aggressively to eclipse Mr. Bessent and become Mr. Trump’s Treasury secretary, at times irritating Mr. Trump in the process.

Mr. Lutnick has had a long relationship with Mr. Trump dating to their days in New York and has proved himself willing to do whatever he thinks Mr. Trump wants, including fighting to put the president’s name on the Kennedy Center and donating $25 million to the future Trump presidential library when his own standing was shaky.

A former bond trader with no government experience, Mr. Lutnick initially deployed the export control powers of his department aggressively, though erratically, on several occasions last year. Those moves prompted harsh reactions from China, upset ongoing trade negotiations and prompted criticism from other top officials.

In September last year, the Commerce Department issued a sweeping rule that added tens of thousands of Chinese companies to the “entity list,” which restricts American companies from exporting products to any company on the list unless they obtain a license from the government to do so. China responded swiftly, by cutting off the supply of rare earth minerals to the United States, which threatened to shutter American factories making cars, tools and other products.

The administration started receiving panicked calls from chief executives, and officials quickly agreed to suspend the rule as part of a trade pact with China. Mr. Lutnick’s employees were then asked to write a short summary for him on what the entity list is.

People familiar with those incidents say Mr. Lutnick was chastened by the blowback. Since then, the department has essentially halted new technology controls against China, concerned that any measures would upset a fragile truce. The department has not issued any entity listings in over a year, the longest stretch of time without an update in 18 years.

Mr. Lutnick’s defenders have repeatedly argued that when it came to Nvidia, he was doing what the president wanted. One person who witnessed a number of discussions about chips policy and Nvidia, who discussed internal deliberations on the condition of anonymity, said that the president was more often than not the person most sympathetic to Mr. Lutnick’s position. Mr. Trump, another official said, wanted to have a good relationship with President Xi Jinping of China.

A third person said the relationship between Mr. Huang and Mr. Lutnick was not always pleasant, including when the commerce secretary took actions that the Nvidia chief did not like.

The growing friendship between Mr. Trump and Mr. Huang of Nvidia also appeared to encourage commerce officials to take a more cautious approach to regulating the company. Mr. Huang has become a frequent guest at the White House, has traveled with Mr. Trump to China, and often speaks on the phone with the president.

Nvidia’s inroads into the White House and the Commerce Department began last year. In the spring of 2025, the Trump administration began pushing forward with a ban on shipments to China of a chip called the H20. Mr. Lutnick told Nvidia that the matter was out of his hands. The company’s only recourse would be to appeal to the president.

Mr. Huang, who was in Florida to receive an engineering award, traveled to Mar-a-Lago for a donor dinner to meet with the president and plead his case.

In April, the ban was issued anyway. But Mr. Huang continued to cultivate his ties with the president. He promised a huge investment in U.S. manufacturing and pledged a donation to the White House ballroom.

By December, Mr. Huang achieved a notable victory. Mr. Trump agreed to allow the company to sell its more advanced H200 chip to China, as long as the U.S. government got a cut of the revenue — an idea that prompted widespread outrage about American national security being for sale. Commerce Department lawyers were deployed to figure out a way to sidestep a U.S. law banning export taxes and realize Mr. Trump’s proposal.

There are also concerns about possible conflicts of interest given that the investment firm that Mr. Lutnick steered for decades, Cantor Fitzgerald, operates in a wide range of industries, from cryptocurrency to data centers, that rely on Nvidia chips and could be affected by rules Mr. Lutnick is currently weighing. That business is now run by Mr. Lutnick’s sons.

Cantor Fitzgerald has served as a financing or placement agent for several companies that are involved in developing or operating data centers in Southeast Asia, like Gorilla Technology Group and Bitdeer Technologies Group, which could be hurt by tougher U.S. limits on chip sales to the region.

The activities of Mr. Lutnick’s sons have been a source of irritation for Mr. Trump and concern for some other Trump advisers, despite the fact that Mr. Trump’s own sons’ businesses have prompted similar criticisms.

The Commerce Department spokeswoman said that Mr. Lutnick had fully divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald and had no interactions or discussions whatsoever with Cantor Fitzgerald regarding Nvidia. Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment.

Mr. Trump and Mr. Lutnick’s closeness with Mr. Huang also reverberated inside the Commerce Department. Top officials appointed by the Trump administration encouraged a more careful attitude toward the company, to the chagrin of rank-and-file employees who wanted to continue the department’s mission.

Mr. Kessler, Mr. Lutnick’s deputy, required communications with the company to be routed through him. Some commerce officials said their bosses had shown little interest in proposed investigations into Nvidia, instead encouraging them to go after Nvidia’s smaller customers.

The department says it has levied far more fines for export control violations than before, and been involved in at least six cases involving smuggling of Nvidia chips, though none of those charges have fallen on Nvidia itself. The department has also refrained from adding Chinese firms that are major Nvidia customers to its entity list, which restricts American companies from exporting products to those companies. The Commerce Department has approved licenses for Nvidia to sell its chips to Chinese firms that The Times found to have links with sanctioned entities or military contractors.

Nvidia also tried to shape the department’s staff. In an effort coordinated by Ned Finkle, the head of external affairs, Nvidia funded opposition research into groups with ties to “effective altruism,” a movement that has sought tighter chip controls as part of an effort to protect humanity from A.I.

The company’s leaders spoke with officials in the administration about effective altruists and complained that there were some at Rand, which had a contract with the Commerce Department to provide a member of the administrative staff. The staff member was dismissed after Nvidia complained that licenses were not being granted for its chip sales to China, these people said.

The tighter ties between Nvidia and the Commerce Department also gave Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, unique influence over the department and its rule-making process. When department staff reviewed drafts of policies under consideration, they sometimes found themselves looking at comments and critiques in the document that had been inserted by Mr. Teter.

With draft rules about the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China, Mr. Teter inserted notes that had the potential to weaken rules that required companies to know who they were selling their chips to, and aimed to influence the volume of shipments allowed to China.

While commerce officials often meet with industry representatives to discuss the impact on business of potential rules, this was viewed as an unusual amount of influence.

A Commerce Department spokesman said it was routine for agencies to consult with companies as they finalize rules. He said the agency aggressively pursues enforcement cases and had never directed staff to refrain from targeting any company. The agency was continuing to consider new entity listings and working with other agencies on that process, he said.

Rob Copeland contributed reporting.

item.title: Microsoft’s Global Outage and Fixes: What We Know
item.description:
Microsoft is reporting widespread improvements to its services after a global outage took them offline on Thursday, disrupting communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world. The company, headquartered in Redmond, Wash., said on Friday that it was seeing “encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure.”

“We remain focused on addressing residual impact and ensuring reliable service restoration,” the company added.

Here’s what to know as of Friday afternoon.

Outages started disrupting Microsoft tools and apps around noon Eastern time on Thursday and quickly spread to more than 70 countries and territories, affecting millions of users, according to Downdetector, an outage-tracking site.

Some of Microsoft’s most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, stopped working.

Microsoft said in a statement on Friday that “for now, we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” It added that the problem was “a technical issue not related to cyber or A.I.” agents.

The company has yet to provide a clear answer, although it has promised to make public a full report that identifies the “root cause” of the outage.

In statements on Thursday and Friday, it provided some details.

Microsoft said on Thursday that “a portion of infrastructure” was experiencing “elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” That could mean that increased stress on its network was caused by a “number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company said.

Microsoft said the servers were failing health checks — periodic, automated assessments that ensure they are functioning correctly and efficiently. It said the failed health checks “may originate from a specific component that’s responsible for processing server health.”

On Friday, Microsoft said the problem had been introduced to the system “during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.” It said it had addressed the underlying issue, allowing its tools and apps to begin to function normally again.

“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” it said. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

Luca Arnaboldi, an assistant professor of cybersecurity at the School of Computer Science at the University of Birmingham in England, said the outage was a reminder that when people use “the cloud,” they are actually relying on servers, which have finite resources.

“In this particular case, as servers became unavailable, capacity on the remaining servers increased, leaving fewer machines to handle the traffic,” he said in a statement. Even after some of the original servers came back online, he added, “the ones currently under strain now fail, creating a constant catch-up.”

Parents struggled to contact their children’s schools, some government services faltered and many office workers could not access email.

The outage affected parts of the federal government, including the U.S. House of Representatives, according to Samantha Carter, a spokeswoman for the office that oversees House operations.

“We have seen improvements to Outlook’s functionality this morning, but will continue to monitor the situation until all issues are resolved and full functionality is restored to all Microsoft applications,” Ms. Carter said in an email on Friday.

Elsewhere in the world, Britain’s National Health Service said the outage was having a “disruptive impact.” The National Pharmacy Association of Britain said the issues at the N.H.S. were making it difficult for pharmacies to communicate with doctors and some patients, which could cause delays in filling prescriptions. The Metropolitan Police in London said its online contact forms weren’t working.

In Australia, intelligence and police forces said that their operations had been affected. Singapore told taxpayers that email had been disrupted, and the Supreme Court of the Philippines and the European Court of Human Rights said the outage could cause delays in its work.

Reporting was contributed by Isabella Kwai, Karla Adam and Adeel Hassan.

item.title: Timing of Climate Science Reports Ignites a Hot Fight at U.N. Talks
item.description:
A squabble over the publication timetable for several climate reports has turned into one of the burning issues of this year’s United Nations climate conference, as some warn that fossil fuel interests might be interfering with the world’s pre-eminent climate science organization.

The U.N.-backed Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change produces landmark reports that generally come out every five to seven years. The next round of reports would take on topics like physical changes to the earth and greenhouse gas emissions.

Timing is critical because in 2028 nations are supposed to assess their progress and then ramp up their efforts to do more, based on the best science. That process, known as a stocktake and occurring every five years, is the engine of the Paris Agreement.

Saudi Arabia, India and Russia are among those pushing to delay the reports so that at least two of them come out after 2028.

The fact that those nations rank among the largest fossil fuel exporters or importers has led to accusations that coal, oil and gas interests might be interfering with science.

“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the I.P.C.C. in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” said former Vice President Al Gore, who is in Turkey for the talks.

At COP31, the United Nations climate talks being held this year in Antalya, Turkey, a handful of world leaders warned that the United Nations’ climate science body is being undermined.

“I am deeply troubled” by the impasse, said Prime Minister Feleti Teo, of Tuvalu, whose island nation lies barely six feet above sea level. “Our survival demands collective actions to be guided by science and not by politics.”

Many small developing nations, as well as the European Union, want all three I.P.C.C. reports to come before this next assessment period so the science can inform new policies. The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, said on Friday that he, too, was in favor of that timetable.

But that group is facing big pushback.

The nations that have sought a delay, which also include China and Kenya, have said they want to ease pressure on government reviewers, according to meeting accounts from the International Institute for Sustainable Development, an independent research organization. Smaller countries without resources have a harder time managing this workload, they say, and faster turnaround time could compromise scientific rigor.

Representatives from Russia, Saudi Arabia, India, China and Iran did not respond to a request for comment.

Patricia Nying’uro, a meteorologist who is Kenya’s lead representative to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, said that Kenya’s position “comes down to capacity, not politics.”

In 2023, countries agreed to transition away from coal, oil and gas. It was the only time a United Nations climate agreement has explicitly referenced fossil fuels.

This year, the Trump administration announced it was withdrawing from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and dozens of other international organizations and treaties, calling them “contrary to the interests” of the United States.

One I.P.C.C. negotiator, who requested anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly, said that in previous years the United States had been a “mediating influence” in talks, one that hasn’t been replaced. In 2013, for instance, Saudi Arabia contested the key findings of a panel’s report but then backed off.

The impasse has complicated the talks in Antalya, which began on Monday.

Diana Acconcia, a senior European Commission climate official, said Friday that if the I.P.C.C. issue were not resolved, it might not be possible for the representatives from 190 countries that have gathered in Turkey to agree on other matters.

“It is not separable from the COP discussions here,” Ms. Acconcia said, adding, “Europe stands on the side of science.”

The climate talks are scheduled to run until Nov. 20.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988, assesses available climate science but does not conduct its own research. It depends on scientists who volunteer to scrutinize existing studies, synthesize findings and draft reports that often span more than 1,000 pages. As part of the timeline fight, its upcoming budget has also been left in limbo.

“Our authors deserve clarity and certainty,” said Jim Skea, a British scientist who chairs the I.P.C.C. “I encourage member governments to spare no effort to find consensus and reach a decision.”
