item.title: ‘Get Focused on London’: How Iran’s Agents Attacked European Targets
item.description:
As the U.S.-Israel war in Iran raged earlier this year, a man linked to Iranian criminal networks perched in front of a computer, on a video call with a teenager in London. The man wanted to make sure the teen, who was moments away from setting fire to a synagogue, carried out his plans.

“Light it up like a Christman tree,” the man, an Iraqi named Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, urged the 17-year-old, according to U.S. prosecutors. The teen climbed over a wall and tossed a bomb through a broken window. “J’s mic is muted,” read the text on Mr. al-Hassani’s computer screen.

The synagogue arson in April was a small, violent part of Iran’s efforts to force an end to the bombing campaign that was pummeling the country, according to American investigators.

The attack was described in a federal indictment filed in New York this week. It revealed extensive new details about a wave of violence against Jewish institutions in Europe and U.S. targets, including a British air base used by American bombers. Prosecutors hold Iran’s agents responsible for the assaults.

Within days of the war starting, Mr. al-Hassani and at least two associates, including an operative for Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, began plotting the attacks in Europe, prosecutors said. The men talked about procuring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. They pored over a map of London, with one saying they should “get focused” on targeting the British capital. Soon after, attacks hit temples and other Jewish sites in London.

In the fight against much stronger conventional forces, Iran has found ways to impose costs on its adversaries without inviting a full military response. One major aspect of Iran’s strategy is its embrace of small-time criminals to conduct low-cost assaults against vulnerable targets that are part of everyday life.

Since the U.S.-Israeli war began, Iran and its proxies — who sometimes act on their own — have stepped up such attacks, particularly in Britain, which has allowed the United States to use its military bases to strike Iranian forces. By hitting American allies, Iran aims to sow fear and try to weaken their support for the U.S. and Israeli military deployments, experts said.

“What we are seeing right now is the application of a playbook Iran has refined over decades,” said Adrian Shtuni, an associate fellow with the International Center for Counter-Terrorism. In addition to the criminal attacks, he also cited Iran’s efforts to build proxy militant networks outside Iran and enhance its abilities to carry out cyberattacks.

The threat persists. This week, as many as a dozen U.S. military aircraft based at R.A.F. Mildenhall in England were evacuated to other bases in Europe, including in Germany, after intelligence officials detected an Iran-backed drone plot against the base, three American officials said.

The Mildenhall air base, about 70 miles northeast of London in Suffolk, is a major hub for U.S. Air Force operations in Europe. It has a large air refueling wing and a Special Operations wing, with about 1,000 military personnel there.

The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, said analysts had received a general warning, but commanders were not taking chances. Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s national security adviser, threatened in an interview on Lebanese television this week to hit U.S. bases in Europe if they are used for attacks against his country.

At the center of Iran’s operations this year in Europe, prosecutors said, is an Iraqi sitting in a Brooklyn jail named Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi. He is a high-ranking commander in Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iran’s most powerful proxies in Iraq. He was captured in Turkey and charged in May with carrying out attacks in Europe and plotting to attack Jewish sites in the United States.

Prosecutors said he also has close ties to the I.R.G.C., the long arm of Iran’s terrorist apparatus.

Mr. al Saadi implored two associates to help him target Europe, investigators said. The I.R.G.C. operative, Mohsen Mohajeri, is an Iranian national. The other, Mr. al-Hassani, is known as “Ali” and has extensive criminal ties according to American court documents.

Days into the war, Mr. al-Saadi and Mr. Mohajeri began conspiring, prosecutors said. It was Mr. Mohajeri who mentioned acquiring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. He sent Mr. al-Saadi a bank account number to buy “equipment for jihad.”

He said he would join Mr. al-Saadi so they could direct the attacks together in Iraq, pledging, “I will not return to Iran until we take revenge.” Mr. Mohajeri traveled to Iraq a couple of days later, and the attacks began in Europe shortly after.

Seven were in Britain, the most of any country. “We need to get focused on London,” Mr. Mohajeri told Mr. al-Hassani in early April while they studied a map of the city on a laptop, according to prosecutors.

Mr. al-Hassani, investigators said, had previously lived in the United Kingdom and had contacts there whom he tapped to carry out attacks.

In an April 15 arson attempt on a synagogue in the London neighborhood of Finchley, investigators said, Mr. al-Hassani spoke over video with a mask-wearing perpetrator. “Go as close as the gate as you can,” he said.

On April 17, all three men were in a room together and on a FaceTime video call with an assailant while he attacked a Jewish charity organization. While the call was projected onto a large screen, Mr. al-Hassani coached the perpetrator to light an incendiary device.

“Light one in your hand,” he said.

“Light it.”

“Throw the fourth one.”

While he directed the attack, Mr. Al-Saadi recorded it. Mr. Mohajeri filmed them both.

The men were behind a new group calling itself HAYI that claimed responsibility for at least six terrorist attacks in and around London, according to court filings. Perhaps the most notorious was the burning of four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer service in Golders Green, a heavily Jewish neighborhood.

In the teenager’s synagogue arson attack in late April, nobody was injured, and the damage was minor. The teen later pleaded guilty and said he did not know it was a temple and that he did not hate Jews.

HAYI has claimed responsibility for about 18 attacks or plots across Europe and the United States in the spring. Mr. al-Saadi also directed blasts against U.S. bank branches in Amsterdam and Paris before he was arrested in May.

As he sat in a jail cell in Brooklyn, Mr. al-Saadi apparently had contingency plans. In conversations with his family in Iraq over the summer, he passed coded messages intended for his two associates, prosecutors said.

In late July, Mr. al-Saadi asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and she replied that it was ongoing.

By August, according to investigators, Mr. al-Hassani was paying accomplices in Britain to initiate an attack on R.A.F. Fairford, the air base that hosted American bombers that flew sorties to Iran. The men — at least five of them — secured vans and barrels of fuel. They researched chemical accelerants and metallic objects that could be used as shrapnel.

Mr. al-Hassani took care to make sure they did the job correctly. He told the men to place custom-made decals on the three vans so they looked like they were part of fuel delivery and swimming pool supply businesses.

They waited for the green light. Investigators say Mr. al-Saadi gave it on Sept. 24, again through his family.

A couple of nights later, Mr. al-Hassani directed the men to drive to the base, talking with them during their journey. But the authorities had been aware of a vague threat to the base. At least two of the vans encountered a security roadblock, blocking the route that Mr. al-Hassani was instructing them to take.

Early in the morning of Sept. 27, the police apprehended the five men and recovered the vans. They never penetrated the base.

But the close call highlighted vulnerabilities in Europe’s security and played into Iran’s effort to raise the cost of Western support for the U.S.-Israeli war.

“They are playing the long game,” Mr. Shtuni said of Iran, “the only one they can.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: A Sweaty, Muddy Jungle Trek to a Famed World War II Wreck
item.description:
Halfway through the morning, I’m being tossed around like a popcorn kernel in the back of a troop carrier playing an eclectic medley of Backstreet Boys and Papua New Guinean jams.

We’re traveling along what feels more like a collection of loose rocks, arranged to be roughly vehicle width, than a road. I’ve lost count of the number of river crossings, including one where the water lapped a few inches from the car’s windows. And this is during a dry spell.

Our caravan is headed for an unlikely tourist destination deep in the jungle on Bougainville Island, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the Solomon Sea.

The piecemeal remnants of a Mitsubishi G4M1 — Betty, as the planes were code-named by the Allies in World War II — have remained for some 80 years at the crash site of Japanese Navy Adm. Isoroku Yamamoto. This is the spot where Admiral Yamamoto, mastermind of the Pearl Harbor attack, archvillain to Americans in the war, a respected and memorialized figure to the Japanese, met his end in 1943.

Bougainville was occupied by the Japanese in early 1942, in the months after Pearl Harbor, as the Imperial Navy pushed into the South Pacific, with Admiral Yamamoto at the helm. In April 1943, Allied forces intercepted and deciphered Japanese communication on the admiral’s travels, and American P-38 Lightning fighters gunned down his plane over southern Bougainville, a feat the Americans triumphantly dubbed Operation Vengeance.

Visiting the relic is not for one faint of heart, time or expense. And yet, war history buffs, Japanese pilgrims, a Chicago hot dog baron and lately, YouTubers, have made the journey, bringing a mix of curiosity, complicated feelings on war and, for many, the desire for bragging rights over going where few have gone.

So far, my journey has involved a flight to Port Moresby, the capital of Papua New Guinea, then a domestic leg to Buka, in the Autonomous Region of Bougainville. From there, it’s a ferry ride across a narrow strait, then four hours by rough, unsealed roads to the coastal town of Arawa. Then, another four hours by even rougher roads, up and over the fog-shrouded Crown Prince Range — to get to the start of the trek into the jungle.

I was in Bougainville with the photographer Matt Abbott to report on the region’s quest for independence, and the lasting legacy of a decade-long civil war that broke out in 1988. On our final day, we made a visit to Admiral Yamamoto’s plane.

I was curious why people would go to such lengths to reach the site. I imagined I might encounter Japanese visitors reflecting on their country’s legacy in World War II, or American or Australian tourists who knew of the place through family lore passed down by Allied servicemen.

As it happened, when I contacted Zhon Bosco Miriona, who runs Bougainville Experience Tours, the group scheduled to make the trip that day was made up of Chinese tourists.

So there we were in three cars — seven Chinese visitors, two journalists, a handful of guides and drivers — making our way to the crash site. As I learned on the bumpy ride, members of the group had found each other online, looking for others game to go off the beaten path.

They were from wildly different walks of life — a cook, a modeling agent, a tech reviewer, a human resources professional, a banker, a woman on a career hiatus and a chemical engineer. Xiaoyu Xu, the engineer, told me he had been to 110 countries, and was making his way through a list of 330 destinations.

Along the way, we got into a minor standoff with villagers over a Japanese tank along the side of the road. The tourists climbed onto the turret, and people from the surrounding village requested 100 kina, about $22. The group balked, and we got back on the road without paying.

“Yumi flow tasol,” I said back in the car, to the amusement of Luke Raupeto, our guide. The Tok Pisin phrase I’d picked up seemed fitting: Just go with it.

Around 2 p.m., the cars made an abrupt turn at a small trading hut. We’d arrived at an idyllic village with thatched roofs, lovingly tended flowers and cocoa beans laid out to dry.

We had reached Kokopo, a hamlet of a few dozen families, ready to begin the trek.

Leading us on the walk was the village chief, Robert Nunu. He said his father was among the people from the village who rushed to the crash site in 1943.

In the immediate aftermath of Admiral Yamamoto’s death, the account told in Japan was that he had perished as a dedicated soldier, found seated upright in the wreckage with a white-gloved hand on his sword. Mr. Nunu said his father had told a different story: that villagers had extracted the admiral badly burned, but still alive. He died later that day, he said.

Historical assessments of the Japanese admiral have also grown more complicated in the intervening years, as it became known how strongly he opposed going to war with the United States, and how he foresaw Japan’s eventual fate in the conflict.

Mr. Nunu was shirtless, in teal-colored galoshes with a machete as long as his arm. We would shortly come to see the wisdom of both. Within 10 minutes, we came across a knee-deep stream. I stripped off socks and boots and rolled up my pants, mosquitoes immediately flocking to my shins. At the next crossing, I gave in and waded, muddy stream water filling my boots, squishing and sloshing with each step. Yumi flow tasol.

A dozen people from Kokopo, including a couple of gleeful children, were along for the trek. We walked through potato fields and among pineapple plants. Our path soon became an overgrown blur of green. Every few steps, one of the villagers equipped with a machete hacked away at a banana leaf or a patch of tall grass.

None of the villagers, save for Mr. Nunu, wore shoes. One of the two women in the tourist group was in a miniskirt and white sneakers that didn’t stay white for long — the other, the agent, sported an orange crop top. (She finished the trek with no mosquito bites on her stomach. I asked.)

Mr. Xu, the engineer, brought three cameras in a large backpack, an action cam strapped to his chest, and a drone in another bag, which one of the villagers carried. The weight wasn’t too much trouble, he said. He’d been to Mount Everest.

After an hour and a half slogging through the vegetation, we came upon a small, unimpressive pile of metal. Don’t worry, this isn’t all of it, Mr. Raupeto said.

A minute later, we came to the main attraction: the crumbling fuselage of the plane, the engine that had broken apart and other fragments strewn through a glade surrounded by encroaching jungle.

Since 1984, the centennial of Admiral Yamamoto’s birth, members of the Yamamoto Admiration Society have been making pilgrimages to the wreck from his birthplace of Nagaoka. They held modest rites of remembrance, with sake and food placed atop a cloth draped over the plane’s remains. Some villagers carried the Japanese visitors piggyback across the streams, recalled Mathias Pihei, who was a regional administrator for the Buin District at the time and facilitated the visits during the 1980s.

“Through them I learned a lot about this man, Yamamoto,” said Mr. Pihei, 74. “As soon as we approached the crash site, they would shout, to greet the spirit.”

If his spirit was there with us, it didn’t make itself known. The tourists busied themselves taking photos of the aircraft, the engine, the interior of the fuselage, climbing the body to pose by the tail fin. The plane’s severed left wing, with the red sun of the Japanese flag, was missing. It was taken from the site to Nagaoka in the late 1980s, and now sits on display in a museum on Admiral Yamamoto. After about a half-hour, Mr. Raupeto started urging us to begin the trek back.

About halfway back, what had been sunny blue skies grew darker and fat droplets of rain started to fall. The villagers hacked off elephant ear fronds to use as umbrellas.

Roc He, 37, the tech reviewer, who has a following of more than 200,000 on Bilibili, one of China’s most popular video platforms, said he didn’t think most Chinese people would understand the desire to come to a place like Bougainville. They would say the money would be better spent on education or on children, he said. He had not told his parents about this trip.

As for the admiral and the plane wreckage, he said the Chinese generally had negative views of the Japanese in World War II, and it made him think about how far their war effort had reached.

I told him having grown up in South Korea myself, the history I was taught was predominantly concerned with the travails of having been colonized by the Japanese and our struggle for independence, and less with the battles far beyond our shores. Not unlike Bougainville, we had been at the mercy of land grabs by outsiders and their contests for dominion, with little heed for the fate of people living in these places.

It was nearly 6 p.m. by the time we were back at the cars. Vinsa Hu, the agent, had logged the return journey on her Apple Watch — 1.5 hours, 240 calories, 4 meters of elevation, 4.3 kilometers (2.7 miles).

Mr. Pihei, the former administrator, said he wished the plane were shielded from the elements so it could stand as a symbol with a message to visitors to Bougainville. The admiral may be associated with Japan’s wartime atrocities for many, but Mr. Pihei said that in the context of Bougainville, still reeling from its own war, the plane could stand for something different.

“When they see the plane, they see peace, because the person who died in the plane was a man of peace. He did not want war,” Mr. Pihei said. “Bougainville, too, does not war anymore. That plane and Bougainville are one. That’s the way I see it.”

item.title: In Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner Ask Putin to Include Europe in Peace Talks
item.description:
President Trump’s envoys went to Moscow on Thursday to seek agreement from President Vladimir V. Putin to bring Europe into talks on the war in Ukraine, as the Kremlin pushes to widen the negotiations to overhaul European security arrangements.

The envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Russia one day after mediating peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, who spoke directly for the first time in nine months. After meeting with Mr. Putin in the Kremlin, the envoys were scheduled to travel to Dublin to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.

Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are pressing to involve Europe in the talks as Russia makes clear that it will not consider a cease-fire until its broader demands to redraw the European security architecture are addressed.

The Trump administration, seeking a foreign policy win after Republicans’ drubbing in the midterm elections, is making another push for peace even as Russia gives no indication that it will stop the war anytime soon, and in fact appears to be hardening some of its positions.

Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of a winter bombing campaign, taking advantage of Ukraine’s lack of air defenses. On Thursday, Mr. Zelensky said that the Ukrainian armed forces were again facing restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet network Starlink, and had asked the United States for information.

For Europe, getting involved in direct negotiations with Russia over Ukraine would be a departure from its long-held position that Russia must stop fighting first. But European officials also insist that the continent must have a seat at the table if talks expand to include crucial questions of Europe’s security.

In his opening remarks at the Kremlin, Mr. Putin told Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner that he was eager to hear their assessments from “a European perspective” after their meetings with representatives of “united Europe.” The two Americans have held a series of meetings with European officials in recent weeks, including in Abu Dhabi.

Mr. Putin has vented at European nations as they have replaced the United States as Ukraine’s biggest backer, asserting that it is Europe, not Russia, that wants war. On Thursday, Mr. Putin signaled to the American envoys that he was not ready for an easy compromise with Europe and that if Russia spoke with its representatives, the negotiations would be tough.

“We would very much like you, distinguished gentlemen, and the American administration as a whole, to work with your European allies so that they finally make up their minds on the question of what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” Mr. Putin said.

The Americans struck more hopeful notes. Mr. Kushner said that the American side had seen “a big change with the Europeans” and that “there is strong momentum and desire to engage together.” Mr. Witkoff said that the American delegation was optimistic that “we can announce shortly” the next trilateral meeting, which “will include the Europeans.”

On Thursday, President Alexander Stubb of Finland said that “there is a real possibility that the Europeans will be around the table, and I think that would be progress in and of itself.” Last month, Mr. Putin held a call with Mr. Stubb and his Norwegian counterpart that some other European leaders denounced as endangering unity on Russia. Europe has struggled to decide who would represent the continent in negotiations.

If Europe joins the talks, said Tatiana Stanovaya, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, it could be interpreted by Mr. Putin as a sign that his tactic of waiting the Europeans out until they begin offering concessions is working.

On Wednesday, speaking at a security conference in Moscow, Aleksei Drobinin, a senior Russian diplomat, outlined a series of proposals that he said could satisfy Moscow’s security demands regarding Europe.

Mr. Drobinin said that Russia could sign bilateral agreements with European states that, “in substance, meet the criteria of mutual nonaggression pacts,” or reach “political agreements on mutually refraining from supporting each other’s adversaries in the event of aggression.” He compared these potential accords to agreements that Russia has signed with Belarus, Iran and North Korea.

The Americans are seeking a sweeping agreement on Ukraine that would bundle questions of a cease-fire, security and territory. Speaking at the Kremlin, Mr. Putin dismissed Ukrainian assertions that he was being fed inflated claims about how much territory Russian troops controlled in Ukraine.

Mr. Putin offered to conduct a humanitarian mission in the Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka, control of which has been contested by Russia and Ukraine. The effort would be similar to the recent cease-fire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Brokered by the U.S. first lady, Melania Trump, that mission was the longest localized cease-fire since 2022 and helped evacuate hundreds of civilians from the town.

The Russian leader said such a mission would also prove a point on Russia’s territorial gains. “At the same time,” Mr. Putin said, “we will see who controls that settlement.”

item.title: In French Election, Centrists Eye a Judo Star and a Central Banker
item.description:
When Teddy Riner, a judo champion and one of France’s most popular athletes, announced this week that he would run for president, it was less a game changer than a welcome diversion. For all of his appeal, Mr. Riner, 37, is unlikely to win the race to replace President Emmanuel Macron next spring.

Yet his quixotic candidacy reveals a hard truth about France’s presidential campaign. Five months before voters go to the polls, many are eager, even desperate, for a fresh face to upend a race that looks increasingly as if it’s on a glide path to the election of France’s first far-right government since World War II.

The main far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, has held a commanding lead over all her rivals for months — a lead that has only been reinforced by weeks of protests, marred by violence, that have shaken France. The most prominent center-right candidate, Édouard Philippe, has faded in the polls as the unrest has sharpened the appeal of far-right calls for law and order and left-wing calls for social justice.

Another beneficiary of the upheaval is a far-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who now appears to be the likeliest candidate to advance into a second round against Ms. Le Pen in France’s two-round system. As things currently stand, French voters would be confronted with a choice between two poles of the political spectrum.

Centrist voters are “afraid of being confronted with a duel between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” said Jean-Daniel Lévy, deputy director of Toluna France, a polling firm. These voters, he said, are an “orphan electorate,” lacking an inspiring candidate, and are “still looking for someone.”

Raphaël LLorca, an analyst at the Jean-Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning research group in Paris, said the search for a white knight showed “the panic of the centrist bloc.” He added, “It is clear that the election is slipping away from them.”

Mr. Riner’s name is not the only one tantalizing frustrated centrists. Christine Lagarde, a French lawyer and former finance minister, announced her resignation as president of the European Central Bank last month, saying she wanted the freedom to weigh in on political debates. She has ruled out a run for the presidency, but that hasn’t stopped French newspapers from speculating that she might still join the race.

Dominique de Villepin, a former foreign minister and prime minister who declared France’s refusal to join the American-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, is weighing a bid. So is François Hollande, a center-left former president who left office in 2017 with the lowest approval rating of any president since France’s current system of government, known as the Fifth Republic, was founded in 1958.

Among declared candidates, two other fresh faces have recently spiked in the polls: David Lisnard, the mayor of Cannes, a socially conservative free marketeer with a slick social media profile; and Raphaël Glucksmann, a left-leaning member of the European Parliament, who recently won a primary among candidates on the center left.What they have in common is that neither worked for Mr. Macron, who, in his waning months in office, is rivaling Mr. Hollande for unpopularity. The three most established center-right candidates — Mr. Philippe, Gabriel Attal and Bruno Retailleau — all served in top jobs in Macron governments. In an election driven by change, analysts say, they are tarnished by that association.

“David Lisnard and Raphaël Glucksmann are not accountable for the past,” said Mr. Lévy, deputy director of the polling firm.

Mr. Lisnard, a onetime journalist who is the son of a professional soccer player, was a vice president of the main right-wing party, the Republicans, and started his own party, New Energy, in 2021. Mr. Glucksmann, a former documentary filmmaker whose father, André Glucksmann, was a famous philosopher, ran for office on a list of Socialist candidates. But he has never been a member of the Socialists, having started his own party, Place Publique, in 2018.

In the most recent poll by Ipsos, Raphaël Glucksmann drew 13 percent, equal to that of Mr. Philippe but behind Mr. Mélenchon, at 17 percent, and Ms. Le Pen, at 33.5 percent. Mr. Lisnard drew 6.5 percent; in other recent polls, he has been as high as 9 percent.

Both men face an uphill struggle, according to analysts: Mr. Lisnard, because he is jostling in a crowded center-right field; Mr. Glucksmann, because the center left has all but withered as a political force in France.

Analysts are also skeptical about a Lagarde candidacy — and not just because she told the French paper La Croix in September that running “would not be a good idea at all.” She cited her age, 70, and the demands of the job.

Philippe Marlière, an expert on French politics at University College London, said Ms. Lagarde’s technocratic style and pro-European tilt would be a liability in an election fueled by populism and nationalism. “This speculation tells us more about the crisis of the French center right,” he said.

Thierry Breton, a former commissioner at the European Union whose name has also come up as a potential candidate, said centrists were struggling because voters were turned off by conventional politicians, with detailed policy agendas, and seemed “willing to vote more and more for a figure or character.”

Enter Mr. Riner, a five-time Olympic gold medalist in judo who has never held elected office. He was born in Guadeloupe, a French territory in the Caribbean, to parents who moved to mainland France in the early 1990s. Mr. Riner has cast his life story as a testament to France’s greatness and vowed to be a unifying force. While his policy positions are a work in progress, he bills himself as a candidate of “neither the right nor the left.”

On paper, he would appear an even longer shot than Ms. Lagarde. But Mr. Lévy noted that Mr. Riner would appeal to younger voters flocking to Mr. Mélenchon, the far-left leader, who has been a fixture at student-led protests. Certainly, none of the candidates can match Mr. Riner’s outsider status.

“I hear anger, which some people echo with a lot of negativity, and from the mouths of people who no longer have ambition or the desire to think big,” Mr. Riner said in an interview with the French paper Le Parisien. “But France is a great country. It allowed me to become the person I am.”

Among those who welcomed Mr. Riner’s campaign was Mr. Macron, who famously emerged as a fresh face midway through the 2017 election. Speaking to a French broadcaster, he said he was “very happy” that Mr. Riner was joining the fray.

“It can only benefit the country,” Mr. Macron said.

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: Border Crossings Have Plummeted. Stephen Miller Isn’t Satisfied.
item.description:
Since President Trump resumed office, the number of illegal crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border has dropped to the lowest point in decades.

For one of Mr. Trump’s top policy advisers, that is not enough.

In conversations with both American and Mexican officials over the last several months, Stephen Miller has insisted that illegal border crossings must be reduced, according to officials in both countries familiar with the private conversations but not authorized to discuss them.

Mr. Miller’s goal, they said, is zero crossings. Mexican officials have said that, with a nearly 2,000-mile border, that is simply not possible.

In his new role as chief of staff, Mr. Miller is expected to continue driving that agenda.

One of the main forums for Mr. Miller’s demands has been his near daily calls with the U.S. ambassador to Mexico, Ronald ​Johnson, some of the officials said. On calls with staff, Mr. Miller, previously the deputy chief of staff, frequently rails about the number of border crossings, despite their low figures, the officials said.

That has been especially true in recent months, they said, as border crossings increased slightly, to the highest point in Mr. Trump’s second term.

Note: Includes encounters outside official border crossings.

Source: U.S. Customs and Border Protection

Sergio Peçanha/The New York Times

Despite illegal-crossing numbers still being low, Mr. Trump has declared and maintained a national emergency at the border. The U.S. military also remains active there.

Mr. Miller’s ascent in the White House may not bode well for the Mexican government. He has for years described Mexico as a source of problems for the United States, including illegal immigrants and drugs, and pushed for hard-line policies in response, including a sweeping deportation campaign and intense pressure on Mexican officials to fight harder against cartels.

Now, in the wake of the Democrats’ triumph in the midterm elections, Mr. Trump appears to be doubling down.

On Thursday, Mr. Trump threatened on social media to double tariffs on Mexico if it did not stop migrant caravans that he called an “INVASION of our country.” Such caravans have been smaller and less frequent in his second term, and have dissolved on their own or been broken up by Mexican officials before the U.S. border.

Andrew Selee, president of the Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan research group, said Mr. Miller would likely keep the White House’s focus on the border. “He wakes up thinking about immigration and Mexico,” he said.

President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico said on Tuesday that Mr. Miller’s promotion wouldn’t affect cross-border cooperation. “The relationship hasn’t changed, even with the change of President Trump’s new chief of staff,” she told reporters.

The Trump administration’s persistent demands on immigration — despite Mexico’s cooperation and the clear results — say a lot about the U.S.-Mexico relationship in the current moment.

Mr. Trump has found some of his biggest second-term successes south of the U.S., including drastically lower border crossings, increasing trade and fewer border fentanyl seizures, which Mexican officials attribute to stepped-up interdiction efforts.

“On day one, President Trump took action to secure our border. He has delivered the most secure border in American history,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman.

Each success, though, has been followed by demands for more.

Just as both U.S. and Mexican officials have said that security cooperation has never been better, the Trump administration once again in recent weeks proposed U.S. military intervention in Mexico — precisely Ms. Sheinbaum’s red line.

Though Mexico has imposed up to 50 percent tariffs on many Chinese imports last year and said it would buy more American goods, Mr. Trump has threatened to cancel the countries’ trade deal, claiming the United States doesn’t need Mexican products.

The story on immigration follows a similar plot.

No country has cooperated more than Mexico on immigration, while also being pushed to deliver more. Under Ms. Sheinbaum, the Mexican government has deployed 10,000 troops to its northern border and intercepted undocumented migrants within the country far before the border.

Mexico has also received more than 320,000 of its own citizens from the United States since Mr. Trump resumed office, according to the Mexican government. The Sheinbaum administration has been very public about welcoming back deported Mexicans and not refusing them.

Another signature strategy of the Trump administration has been deporting immigrants to countries that are not their own. It has attracted headlines and criticism for sending Latin Americans to Africa, for instance. Mexico has accepted roughly 21,000 deportees from other nations, nearly all from seven Latin American countries, according to Mexican government data.

That is about 80 percent of the total third-country deportees, said Savi Arvey, an official at Human Rights First, an immigrant advocacy group that tracks deportations. The other roughly 5,000 such deportees went to 28 other countries.

Mexico has been quiet about its cooperation on the policy, while dealing with its headaches. It has allowed a majority of deportees to remain in Mexico, but it has been challenging. The Mexican government knows little about the migrants it receives, such as people with chronic health conditions or those who say they will face torture in their home countries, said Gretchen Kuhner, director of the Institute for Women in Migration, a nonprofit that aids deportees in Mexico.

Most of those migrants are Cubans, Venezuelans and Guatemalans, Ms. Kuhner said. Many will remain in Mexico, she added, and could face exploitation if they lack proper residence or work permits.

While Mexico has received deportees from other countries, the United States has also been deporting Mexicans elsewhere. Nearly 4,000 Mexicans have been sent to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica, according to Mexican government data, despite protests from the Mexican government.

Ms. Sheinbaum has expressed anger with those moves. “There is no reason for them to send nationals to any Central American country,” she said in an August news conference. “No reason whatsoever.”

The United States also sent two Mexicans to Eswatini, according to human rights groups, and another to South Sudan, Ms. Sheinbaum said.

This happened despite Mexico’s cooperation at the border.

Under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., illegal crossings surpassed a record of roughly 8,200 a day in December 2023. It became a national controversy, regularly stressed by Fox News pundits, and helped Mr. Trump and other Republicans sweep to power in the 2024 election.

Yet before that vote, the Biden administration and the Mexican government worked to slow the flow of migrants. By the time Mr. Trump took office, crossings averaged 950 a day. Then, in July 2025, they hit the lowest points in several decades: 150 crossings a day, according to government figures.

Since March, the numbers inched back up. Over the past seven months, the monthly average has been about 300 illegal crossings per day, partly driven by Mexican migrants.

Ms. Sheinbaum has sought to remind Mr. Trump on their frequent phone calls that Mexico is cooperating on immigration, according to people familiar with the calls who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations. That has included sending him graphics that show the drop in border crossings, as well as noting that she has kept her promise to him that no migrant caravan would make it to the U.S.-Mexico border, these people said.

In response to the Trump administration saying in June that it was delivering “the most secure border in American history,” Ms. Sheinbaum said, “there couldn’t be a secure border if we don’t work from both sides, without collaboration: the United States on their side and us on our side.” She also highlighted a drop in fentanyl crossing the border.

Mr. Trump told “60 Minutes” last week that his immigration policies may have gone too far and that he was open to working with Democrats on an immigration deal.

“It both helped and hurt,” he said of his policies. “I got an A-plus for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Then he promptly gave Mr. Miller more influence.

Roberto Lazzeri, Mexico’s ambassador in Washington, said in a recent interview that Trump administration officials have floated ideas about what more the Mexican government can do to control immigration. But “nothing specific” has been asked, he said.

He suggested one possible way the United States could help, though: If the Trump administration has information about which communities migrants are coming from, Mr. Lazzeri said, the Mexican government could “maybe put additional oversight work” into those hot spots.

“That’s something that we can do more,” he said. “What we won’t do is just go against our frameworks and our laws.”

Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting from Washington, Jody García from Guatemala City, and Miriam Castillo and Emiliano Rodríguez Mega from Mexico City.

item.title: After Xi Purges China’s Generals, a Military Inquisitor Rises
item.description:
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, endorsed the expulsion of dozens of disgraced officials at a recent Communist Party meeting in Beijing, one man stood out as a clear winner.

Taking his new place at the front of the meeting was Gen. Zhang Shengmin, the somber-faced enforcer of Mr. Xi’s purges inside the military. He had been promoted to the Politburo, the party’s top leadership council, the latest step in his improbable rise from low-profile inspector to a position second only to Mr. Xi in China’s military hierarchy.

General Zhang has been the principal overseer of Mr. Xi’s campaign to purify the People’s Liberation Army. His latest elevation signaled that the investigations, indoctrination drives and loyalty tests could continue for years, as Mr. Xi searches for officers he believes are irreproachably loyal, experts and officials said.

“Twist the blade inward, with strict measures to cure disorder,” China’s main military newspaper said after the party meeting that was held late last month, referring to the continued discipline campaign.

Three officials in Taiwan said they believed Mr. Xi’s loyalty campaign would keep the Chinese military focused on its own problems. That could hinder preparations for possible war over Taiwan, the self-governed island democracy that Beijing claims. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal assessments.

The leadership uncertainty comes as China’s military has continued to pressure Taiwan. Dozens of P.L.A. ships held unannounced drills in seas off the Chinese coast in recent weeks, with some, including a carrier strike group, still remaining, Joseph Wu, the secretary-general of Taiwan’s National Security Council, posted on X on Thursday.

But the exercises appeared less sophisticated than earlier ones — potentially reflecting disruptions to the P.L.A. command, another Taiwanese official said. He spoke on the condition of anonymity, citing rules about sharing military intelligence with reporters.

John Culver, a former Central Intelligence Agency analyst who studied the Chinese military, said that “Xi’s animating motivation isn’t war or preserving his own power as goals in and of themselves.”

“It’s saving the party, and ensuring that the P.L.A. will fulfill its role as the armed wing of the Chinese Communist Party,” said Mr. Culver, a nonresident senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, referring to the People’s Liberation Army.

General Zhang’s promotion was unusual. He was the first official in 32 years to join the Politburo outside its regular five-year leadership cycle.

He has scant experience in leading military operations. He was for many years a political officer, enforcing party rule over the military, and then an investigator hunting for corruption and misbehavior. Outside the military, he became best known for his Chinese brushstroke calligraphy.

His rise is the story of Mr. Xi’s declining faith in many of his handpicked generals. Dozens have been removed, often accused of corruption and betraying Mr. Xi’s orders.

General Zhang has no elite family background or powerful patrons in the armed forces, said Joseph Torigian, an associate professor at American University in Washington who studies China’s political and military elites.

“Xi Jinping has lost trust in so many people, but he maintains trust in this one person and may want to keep him around simply because a good deputy is so hard to find,” Mr. Torigian said.

But he noted the risks for General Zhang. “It’s going to be tough politics for Zhang Shengmin to manage, because if you’re the only one, you have to be so careful to not raise doubts in the top leader,” he said.

In Taiwan, many observers expect China to step up its military pressure on the island if its president, Lai Ching-te, wins another term in elections in early 2028. Beijing has denounced Mr. Lai for rejecting its claims of sovereignty over Taiwan.

But the leadership upheaval in the Chinese military could make it harder for Mr. Xi to marshal a full suite of military options against Taiwan, possibly for years, experts said.

“Because going to war demands certain victory, he harbors no illusions about the severe leadership deficit hollowing out the Liberation Army,” Ma Cheng-kun, a professor at the National Defense University in Taiwan who studies the People’s Liberation Army, said at a recent seminar in Taipei.

“Fully replenishing personnel cannot be done that rapidly,” Professor Ma said, “especially when virtually all generals, well-qualified senior officers, are gone.”

Mr. Xi controls the armed forces as chairman of the Central Military Commission, a council that has usually included six or more senior commanders. After the expulsion of five members, the commission is now made up of just Mr. Xi and General Zhang.

General Zhang enlisted in the military in 1978 and for decades served as a political commissar, instilling the party’s values in troops and rooting out those who violated its rules.

In the 1980s, as Deng Xiaoping opened China’s economy to a commercial boom, General Zhang, then a junior officer in northwest China, wrote about the threat the changes posed to military discipline. He warned that relationships in the armed forces were being warped by greed. “Some can fulfill their individual interests and aspirations only by relying on personal connections,” he and a co-author wrote in a paper in 1988.

Outside the military, General Zhang earned a reputation for his calligraphy. He often wrote “cursive script,” or cao shu — a free-flowing style that exudes spontaneity.

At work, though, General Zhang focused on discipline and obedience. After Mr. Xi came to power in 2012, General Zhang echoed Mr. Xi’s warnings that corruption was sapping the army’s fighting strength. By then, he was an officer in the Second Artillery, the missile force that would later emerge as a nest of corruption scandals.

“The conduct of senior officers is a barometer in the military,” General Zhang wrote in a military journal in 2014. “If leading officers pursue pleasure and wallow in luxury, that seriously harms the relationship between officers and troops and undermines cohesion and combat effectiveness of the military.”

In 2015, he was promoted to a position under the Central Military Commission. Two years later, he was made head of the military’s Discipline Inspection Commission, which investigates corruption and disloyalty, and promoted to full general rank with a seat on the Central Military Commission.

Even so, he remained overshadowed by the more senior commanders leading China’s rapid military buildup.

That began to change in 2023, when investigators under his authority targeted China’s missile force and ousted commanders accused of corruption. The investigations spread to other arms of the military and to higher levels of its hierarchy.

As the scandals spread, General Zhang became increasingly important to Mr. Xi’s renewed drive to clean out generals accused of defying him and taking bribes.

That campaign reached a peak early this year, when Gen. Zhang Youxia, China’s most senior uniformed officer, was placed under investigation, along with Gen. Liu Zhenli, the chief of the Joint Staff Department. One theory is that their violations included questioning Mr. Xi’s proposal to elevate General Zhang Shengmin to the position of vice chairman of the military commission. He gained that position in October.

General Zhang’s latest promotion to the Politburo raised the possibility that he could remain as China’s top general after a Communist Party congress late next year, when Mr. Xi is all but sure to win a fourth term in power. At 68 now, General Zhang would be older than usual to stay in office, but Mr. Xi has set aside retirement norms for some officials. Still, the purges are a warning that not even those close to Mr. Xi are secure.

General Zhang “could be discarded at any point,” said Mr. Culver, of the Brookings Institution. “If there’s one lesson we should have drawn, it is that there are no essential Xi allies.”

item.title: Europe Haggles Over Who Will Represent It in Talks With Russia
item.description:
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. Now they finally expect to get one, and they don’t know who should sit in it.

“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and one of his two envoys, said on Thursday.

Mr. Kushner’s dig reflected a harsh — and, for Europe, potentially embarrassing — reality that internal divisions could cost European officials time and influence. Mr. Kushner and his fellow lead U.S. negotiator, Steve Witkoff, pushed this week to add the Europeans to the talks after Russia insisted during discussions in the United Arab Emirates that postwar security in Europe be a topic of negotiation.

Russian negotiators made it clear during the talks with Ukraine and the United States that as a condition of ending the war, they want Europe to change how it protects itself. Russia has a record of pushing to pare back NATO operations near its border.

European officials have rejected those suggestions, insisting that the continent, not the Kremlin, decides its own security. But Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff expressed openness to expanding the scope of the talks to try to break the impasse on discussions about the war.

“I don’t want someone to talk about our European house, if they are not living in that house,” Luc Frieden, prime minister of Luxembourg, said in an interview on Friday.

Naming a lead negotiator would give Europe a voice in discussions about its own future, while failing to identify someone quickly might make the continent appear weak and fragmented. How the Ukraine war is settled could reverberate across Europe for decades — either containing the threat of Russian expansionism or emboldening it.

“Europe really needs to pay attention,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine warned dozens of leaders from across the continent assembled in Dublin for a summit on Thursday. European Union leaders will debate who should represent them on Friday at a lunch in the Irish capital. Mr. Zelensky is pushing Europe to choose someone by the end of the month, possibly as soon as a meeting of Ukraine’s allies next Thursday in Germany.

The issue grew more pressing late on Thursday. Mr. Kushner told reporters at an air base in Dublin, after a meeting with the Kremlin, that Russian officials had been asked about having European negotiators at the table and were “willing to give it a try.” Mr. Zelensky, standing alongside him, added that “next time, next meeting,” Europe will be on the “negotiation team.”

Even with such high stakes, picking a representative, or even a small group to speak for Europe, has become a herculean lift.

Small nations in the European Union do not always trust big ones to reflect their interests. Britain and Norway, which have a financial and security stake, are not part of the union. Eastern nations bordering Russia doubt that western ones understand the depth of the menace they face.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland said on Thursday, “Under no circumstances will we allow new security rules for this part of the world to be established over our heads, without Poland or Europe having a say.”

European officials have already warned not to expect an immediate choice, though nominations are pouring in.

António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, comes up frequently as a possibility. Mr. Frieden, the Luxembourg prime minister, has suggested that Mr. Costa should be the bloc’s representative. Prime Minister Andrej Babis of the Czech Republic threw out a handful of names, including Mr. Tusk and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy.

Several leaders suggested that they were more likely to settle on a group than a single person.

“It’s not necessarily one person, but there should be a clear, coherent leadership, from the European Union, at that table,” Micheal Martin, the Irish leader, told reporters this week.

One possibility could be a team of negotiators from Europe’s large nations, Britain and NATO, led by Mr. Costa as a central figure. Mr. Costa himself alluded to a potential grouping.

“Europe’s security cannot be discussed without a European voice at the table — that European voice needs to be a team effort between European nations, the European Union and NATO,” he said.

Two European diplomats said that one concern is that Mr. Costa may lack the international stature to impress the Russians and Americans. The diplomats spoke on condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

Mr. Costa has long argued that the European Union must be represented in discussions because the bloc controls a large set of sanctions against Russia, which Moscow wants rolled back. Another factor is Ukraine’s potential E.U. membership, which Kyiv wants as a security guarantee.

Complicating matters, many European officials have opposed even opening discussions with Russia before Moscow agrees to a cease-fire.

When Mr. Costa’s office tried in June to reopen lines of communication with Russia, France and Germany criticized him for overreaching.

These discussions might unfold differently, the two European diplomats suggested, because the chance of sitting at the table now seems realistic and Europe’s security is clearly on the line.

“We will figure out who to represent Europe,” Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Denmark said on Thursday. “In democracies, there will be discussions, but I’m pretty sure we will find a way forward.”

That doesn’t mean it won’t be tumultuous.

item.title: Study Hard, Get a Career, Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
item.description:
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.

In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.

In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.

In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.

It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.

The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

In many places around the world, that system has proved to be remarkably effective, in large part because education has translated relatively straightforwardly into economic mobility.

But increasingly, many who work hard at higher education, often going into debt and sacrificing years of earnings potential to do so, are finding that the rewards are not there at the end. Instead of expected winnings, many young people are greeted with a life of economic struggle.

This discontent is affecting politics elsewhere as well. In the United States, data from The New York Times showed that 70 percent of voters under 30 in the recent midterm elections cast their ballots for Democrats, who tapped educated young people’s widespread frustration over being saddled with debt and stuck in low-paid, dead-end jobs.

In Serbia, student protests grew into a political movement that ousted Aleksandar Vucic, the country’s longtime nationalist strongman, in an election last month. And young people across Europe are set to walk out on Nov. 20 in a general strike that could disrupt schools and businesses throughout the continent.

An even bigger threat looms on the horizon, one that could upend the bargain everywhere: A.I. promises to dramatically restructure, or perhaps sever completely, the relationship between education and well-paid work.

That has the potential to further challenge not only the distribution of economic rewards, but the political bargain on which modern societies have been built.

Historically, such moments have been explosive — even revolutionary.

The version of the meritocratic bargain we see today, with university education as a primary filter for middle-class careers, is a relatively recent construct, and not to be taken for granted.

Britain didn’t introduce universal, free secondary education until 1944. In the United States, college was largely the province of the privileged few until the G.I. Bill opened access to veterans after World War II. Around the same time, the SAT created the first nationally standardized benchmark for admissions.

In countries whose economies developed later, the bargain took even longer to take shape. In India, the national college entrance exam was not introduced until the 1960s. In China, there is a long history of using meritocratic exams to select civil servants and other elites, but that system was disrupted by 20th-century reforms and the Cultural Revolution. The modern system was ushered in by Deng Xiaoping. In 1977 he re-established the national “gaokao” exam system as part of a post-Cultural Revolution rebuilding process. In the late 1990s, further reforms radically expanded university access.

For individuals, this access to education promised more money, more status or both. But for governments, it also offered political stability — a way to convince people to buy into society as currently structured, by promising the potential for advancement to the underprivileged without ousting those who had wealth and power already.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

Research has shown that the prospect of upward mobility — sometimes abbreviated as POUM — can make the poor less likely to demand redistribution. In China, merit-based selection for civil service jobs made people more willing to tolerate inequality, Hanzhang Liu, a political scientist at Florida State University, has found.

When people believed the system was meritocratic, they were more likely to attribute their failures to their own poor abilities, or to the high quality of the competition, she said. But when they did not believe so, those who lost out on jobs were more likely to consider the system rigged.

Still, education-based meritocracy puts significant burdens on the young people working to advance, and on their families. In India, students often go into debt and spend years of grueling study to try to win spots at the most prestigious engineering and medical programs.

In South Korea, national tests have generated an entire industry of cram schools known as hagwons, where students toil for hours each day on top of their regular schoolwork. In the United States, networks of charter schools like KIPP popularized the idea that for poor, ambitious kids, “college starts in kindergarten.” And when actual college starts, American students can easily take on six-figure debts for their degrees.

Just as the meritocratic bargain can be a source of social cohesion, a breakdown can become a trigger for social explosion.

In 1905, China abolished the national civil service exam that had for 1,300 years been a major way to recruit elites, including government bureaucrats. That move came as a shock to the people who had invested in years of education, hoping to earn a privileged position in society.

Those shattered expectations contributed to the revolutionary uprisings that eventually overthrew the imperial dynasty in 1911, according to the economists Ying Bai, at the University of Hong Kong, and Ruixue Jia, at the University of California, San Diego.

In an influential 2016 paper, they found that frustrated commoners who had hoped to become elites via the exam were especially likely to join the revolution. Disillusioned scholars flocked to revolutionary organizations in search of alternative routes to advancement, and became a major force behind the revolt.

That is not to say that France’s unrest signals the imminent return of the guillotine. But the recent protests there, and in other European countries like Italy and Spain, were fueled, in part, by the sense that the old order was enriching itself at the expense of providing opportunities for young people.

Much the same can be said of the student protest movement that led to the election defeat of Mr. Vucic in Serbia, where angry young people felt that meritocratic opportunity had been crowded out by corruption.

Protests can be a blunt instrument. But data show that the demonstrators have a point. In Europe, high unemployment rates for young people, paired with skyrocketing costs of living, have put the traditional milestones of independent adulthood out of reach for many.

Even in countries with healthier economies, there are signs that the breakdown of the meritocratic bargain is already having political consequences. In India, economic growth has been stronger, but it has not created enough jobs to keep up with the expansion of higher education.

In the United States, the emphasis on higher education as a sorting mechanism has led to people pouring tens of thousands of dollars into degrees that no longer necessarily confer economic advancement but still charge as if they do. Discontent has fueled the rise of political movements like the Democratic Socialists of America and efforts to unionize the work forces of companies like Starbucks and Amazon, Noam Scheiber, a Times labor reporter, writes in his new book, “Mutiny: The Rise and Revolt of the College-Educated Working Class.”

But the biggest blow to the meritocratic bargain may be yet to come, as many fear that A.I. could do for knowledge work what a meteor strike once did for the dinosaurs.

A.I.’s arrival has already wiped out some entry-level technical jobs. In the United States, young coders are finding themselves working at Chipotle rather than starting the highly paid tech careers they had expected.

Even if A.I. does not eliminate professionals like lawyers, scientists and doctors, it may radically reshape those fields — and perhaps slash the salaries that come with them.

Some professions may adapt by making greater use of A.I. tools, even as other careers see their pay and numbers collapse. With time, new educational structures may also develop to match skills and meritocratic selection to the demands of a new economy.

But such profound economic change is by its very nature disruptive. In the meantime, it is likely to sow even more confusion about how young people can set themselves up for success, or prevent themselves from sliding down the economic ladder.

item.title: The U.S.-Israel Relationship Is Broken. Here’s How Eisenkot Could Fix It.
item.description:
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form Israel’s new governing coalition and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is by no means assured of success.

But if he does take power, another hugely daunting challenge would immediately confront him: how to undo the vast damage done to Israel’s relationship with the United States, its closest and most important ally.

It’s hard to imagine things getting much worse.

Many Americans have turned against Israel over its devastating military campaign in Gaza, and even more so over its role in pressing for war with Iran, which led to soaring gas prices.

President Trump announced this month that he would cut off billions of dollars in annual U.S. military aid to Israel by the end of the year and blamed Israel in part for Republican losses in the midterm elections. Democratic control of Congress could quickly lead to sanctions on violent Israeli settlers and on new settlement construction in the occupied West Bank, as well as to new conditions on arms sales.

In the past, Israel could always turn to Congress for support in clashes with the White House, said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to Washington and deputy prime minister under Mr. Netanyahu. But no longer.

“For the first time in the history of our relationship with the United States, we have no recourse,” he said. “We have to start from scratch. We have a lot of fence mending to do and with no guarantee of success. Zero.”

Mr. Eisenkot is also unlikely to enjoy much of a grace period in Washington, Senator Chris Coons, the Delaware Democrat expected to become chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in January, said in an interview. Asked how much time a new Israeli government would be given to make substantive moves toward repairing ties, he replied: “Not much. Not years.”

“I’m going to work to try and restore and sustain bipartisan support for Israel,” Senator Coons said. “But that support is more likely to be possible if we see Israel making changes in policy that move in the direction of our shared values.”

Interviews with more than a dozen former Israeli and U.S. ambassadors, lawmakers, analysts and other experts on U.S.-Israeli ties — nearly all of whom were rooting for Mr. Eisenkot to succeed — reveal a broad consensus on steps he could take in the short term to demonstrate his desire to fix things.

But each of those moves carries risks.

Particularly outrageous to many Americans and damaging to Israel’s image, experts in both countries say, is what Mr. Eisenkot has called “Jewish terrorism.” By this he has meant the mounting wave of often lethal attacks against unarmed Palestinians across the West Bank by extremist Israeli settlers, acting with virtual impunity.

Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli consul general in New York, said Mr. Eisenkot had to begin by keeping a campaign promise to crack down on settler violence — and with “zero tolerance.”

Avishay Ben Sasson-Gordis, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, said that stopping settler violence was merely the “table stakes” needed to “start a conversation” in Washington.

Experts said Mr. Eisenkot also would need to keep his promises to uproot Israeli settlements in parts of the West Bank designated to be under Palestinian control and to halt the development of a tract of land outside Jerusalem known as E1. Critics say that building there would make a contiguous Palestine state in the West Bank impossible.

As for the Gaza Strip, Shira Efron, an Israeli analyst at RAND, said Mr. Eisenkot needed to “flood the zone with aid” and put a priority on providing Gazans, most of whom have been displaced by the war, with shelter. “The images from Gaza have to stop,” she said. “We have to show we have no interest in hurting the civilians of Gaza.”

Senator Coons, too, said Israel’s next government needed to allow tents and tent poles into Gaza, “particularly as winter is setting in.”

Mr. Pinkas suggested going further. “I’d instruct the military to build three field hospitals to treat Palestinian children,” he said. “It’s cheap, it’s the right thing to do, it’s the humane thing to do, and it’d win praise from both Trump and the new Congress.”

Any of these moves would mark a striking U-turn from Israel’s current policy. All of them would provide fresh talking points to Israel’s defenders in the United States, who say they are desperate for some.

But they all carry political risks for Mr. Eisenkot. Mr. Netanyahu and his right-wing allies would most likely use any concessions — like lifting Israel’s economic chokehold on the Palestinian Authority, another Eisenkot campaign promise — to denounce Mr. Eisenkot for caving in to international pressure, Ms. Efron said.

“The low-hanging fruit is settler violence,” she said. “Most of the Israeli public is opposed to that.” But if government efforts to arrest extremist settlers or uproot West Bank settlements led to violence, “that would be more controversial,” she said.

A new government should frame its actions as a sharp change in direction, experts said, reversing Mr. Netanyahu’s drive toward annexation of the West Bank and reviving the possibility of a Palestinian state beside Israel one day.

Even if the government’s initiatives encountered domestic resistance in Israel, that would help elicit good will, and buy time, in Washington, experts said.

“It would not be difficult for the incoming Israeli government to show that it’s taking courageous steps and needs the support of Americans, and not their sanctions,” said Ted Sasson, a scholar of U.S.-Israel ties who divides his time between Tel Aviv and Middlebury, Vt.

The Israeli government also needs to change the way it talks about its future, experts said. Rather than arguing why peace can’t be achieved, officials should describe the peace they yearn for.

“Eisenkot has to get up there and say we’re devoted to peace,” said Mr. Oren, the former ambassador. “We haven’t sung that music in a long, long time, and music is important here.”

Daniel Shapiro, who was President Obama’s ambassador to Israel, said Mr. Eisenkot could quickly make clear that Israel — while still recovering from the trauma of the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, and determined to defend itself — was willing to pursue peace and “understands that trauma was also visited on the Palestinians.”

“Those are notes we haven’t heard,” Mr. Shapiro said. “It wouldn’t take a weekly Fox News appearance to establish that that’s the idiom of the new Israeli government and the face it’s presenting to the American public.”

At the same time, experts said that Mr. Eisenkot would need to prepare Israelis for stark policy shifts. Tal Becker, a former chief legal adviser at Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, warned that moving too fast could provoke significant opposition from the Israeli right.

“Before you realize your dreams,” he said, “you need to reassure your opponents that you’re not planning on realizing their nightmares.”

Rebooting the U.S.-Israel alliance would require face time for Mr. Eisenkot in Washington. But Daniel Kurtzer, a former U.S. ambassador to Israel in the George W. Bush administration, urged an earlier trip — to the Arab capitals of Cairo, Amman and Abu Dhabi.

“Get them on board with the idea that change has really happened,” he said of leaders there. “And then you come to Washington reflecting not just parochial Israeli interests” but having galvanized a coalition that could help Mr. Trump across the region.

Other moves could be seen as gifts to Mr. Trump, experts said. These could include negotiating a possible Israeli pullback from territory held in Lebanon and Syria. Or they could include acquiescing to a U.S. deal with Iran that restores calm and reopens the Strait of Hormuz, without Israel dropping its insistence that Iran’s nuclear program be addressed.

Mr. Eisenkot also could begin cooperating with Mr. Trump’s Gaza peace plan unveiled last year, experts said, for instance by easing Israel’s insistence that Hamas fully disarm before the Israeli military begins to withdraw.

Mr. Kurtzer said that Mr. Eisenkot could take a symbolic first step by pulling Israeli troops back slightly inside Gaza and then rely on Mr. Trump to force Hamas to begin decommissioning its weapons.

Mr. Eisenkot has even more ground to make up with Democrats in Congress than with the White House, after more than a decade during which Mr. Netanyahu aligned himself with Mr. Trump and the G.O.P., experts said. (Mr. Coons, unprompted, recalled how offended he had been by Mr. Netanyahu’s 2015 address to Congress in opposition to President Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal.)

“He’s got to make a convincing case to mainstream Democrats that Israel no longer votes Republican, that it’s bipartisan,” Mr. Kurtzer said.

Mr. Eisenkot tried to reassure right-wing Israeli voters that he didn’t see the creation of a Palestinian state on the horizon. But that will not play so well in Washington.

Leaders of J Street — the liberal pro-Israel lobby that has gained influence with Democrats — have made clear they will not wait around. The group says it will continue to press for Israel to accede to the creation of a Palestinian state.

“The world wants it tomorrow,” said Nadav Tamir, the group’s top official in Israel. “The train has left the station. And the expectation that America has to give Israel time and a grace period is not connected to reality.”

It remains uncertain whether Mr. Eisenkot will be able to build a governing coalition; and if he does, whether his cabinet would include ministers opposed to policy changes desired in Washington.

Tzipi Livni, a former Israeli foreign minister, said she hoped that Americans would give a new government the benefit of the doubt.

“Clearly, we need to be quick,” Ms. Livni said. “I hope we will be given a chance, a period of time. But I’m not sure that we have that much time.”

item.title: Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other
item.description:
So many people are dying of Ebola that their bodies have been stacked, one atop the other, on makeshift racks in a shed by the hospital gate.

The town’s main cemetery is full, so fresh graves are being squeezed in between palm trees by the side of the road.

Medicine, IVs and basic protections have been so scarce that three-quarters of Ebola patients in this besieged Congolese town have died.

Supported by

The new epicenter of Congo’s fast-spreading outbreak is a region scarred by rebel violence. Responders are struggling to help it.

By Declan Walsh

Photographs by Daniel Berehulak

Declan Walsh and Daniel Berehulak have traveled for weeks through remote towns in eastern Congo to track the spread of Ebola.

Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province.

It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as its moves through one of the world’s great rainforests.

Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain.

Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

“We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.”

And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

Ebola was already swamping Biakato when I got to the town in mid-October with the photographer Daniel Berehulak. Exhausted health workers reported 300 cases in the span of a month, up from 20 the month before.

But there were only two doctors, they hadn’t been paid in months, and they felt utterly abandoned. The aid workers who would normally pour in and set up an Ebola treatment center were being scared off by rebel fighters who have been terrorizing the region for years.

Their fears were tragically realized in recent days when the rebels, who are affiliated with the Islamic State, killed 106 people in a series of attacks across the region, U.N. officials said. One of the deadliest episodes occurred 25 miles south of Biakato, where militants torched homes, shops and health facilities, forcing Ebola patients to flee their beds. Thousands of residents also fled in an exodus likely to further spread the disease.

Even by the standards of eastern Congo, where conflict has raged for three decades, the fighters — from a group called the Allied Democratic Forces, or A.D.F. — are considered especially brutal. They roam the sprawling forests, periodically springing from their hiding places to mount attacks. Civilians are beheaded, mutilated and abducted. Children are forced to fight with the group. Mass killings have taken place at funerals and churches.

In 2019, the group pledged allegiance to the Islamic State, and by one recent estimate, it is the world’s second-deadliest group for civilians. Now, its terror tactics are hobbling the fight against Ebola.

A tentative effort to rescue Biakato is underway. Aid groups are using helicopters to fly over the perilous forests and have begun to build a treatment center. Even so, the local volunteers battling to hold back the tide of infections say they are in an impossible bind.

“We’ve got the A.D.F. on one side, and Ebola on the other,” said Jean-Lefranc Sakara, head of a Red Cross team that collects the Ebola dead from their houses. “We are well and truly caught in the middle.”

Daniel and I reached Biakato after a jolting two-hour ride through the rainforest. A wall of trees rose on either side, interrupted in places by ghost villages, their deserted buildings barely visible behind grass and weeds.

The fighters started preying on this forested corridor five years ago, ambushing passing traffic and raiding settlements. Most residents have since fled.

“It wasn’t safe for children any more,” said a man who suddenly emerged from the bushes, “so everyone moved to Biakato.” He hurried away, vanishing into the tall grass.

This muddy track, running 85 miles through the rainforest, has become the central artery of the outbreak. Cases are soaring in the towns of Beni and Mambasa, at either end of the road. Halfway along it lies Biakato.
